DAUGHTERS OF ST. ANNE.

God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno.

ROME 1994.

IMPRIMATUR

From the Vicariate of Rome, 4-2-1994.

REMIGIO RAGONESI Titular Archbishop of Ferento Vicegerent of Rome.

© March 25, 1994.

by Congregation of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Via Merulana, 177 – 00185 ROME

Printed by S.G.S. – Via Umbertide, 11 – Tel. 78.27.819 – 00181 Rome Printing completed: March 1994.

The task which the Second Vatican Council entrusted to every religious family, of going back to the sources of its own spirituality in order to draw renewed vigor from its original inspiration, is the reason for this publication on “God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno.”

The Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne, is one of the most eminent figures among the foundresses of the last century. She is also a mystic of a high order.

She was born in Genoa, the City which Leo XIII called Ager fertilis for having given the Church, among other saints, three outstanding figures who consecrated themselves totally to God in widowhood, were endowed with lofty mystical gifts and, at the same time, were animators and guides of movements or of religious families: Saint Catherine of Genoa (1447-1510), foundress of the Work of the Company of Divine Love; Blessed Maria Vittoria De Fornari Strata (1562-1617), foundress of the Order of the Most Holy Annunciation; Blessed Virginia Centurione Bracelli (1587-1651), foundress of the Sisters of Our Lady of Refuge on Mount Calvary.

In this category our Servant of God, Rosa Gattorno, may well be placed as the fourth, even though she, unlike the others, worked outside Genoa, in Piacenza and in Rome.

God’s plan is carried out in this exceptional creature through three states of life: marriage, widowhood, religious life.

In this last state there would come about her radical involvement in God and in Christ, which would mature into a spiritual depth whose bottom is hard to reach. In her, in Rosa Gattorno, there is infused knowledge of the mysteries and, in particular, a singular penetration of the Trinitarian Mystery. In her there are particular insights into certain aspects of the Divine Fatherhood: the Father who converses with his creature; the Father who casts down and who consoles.

In the mystical experience of Rosa Gattorno, the Son, the Incarnate Word, reveals himself above all as Teacher of Wisdom, the Beloved, the Well-Beloved of the Song of Songs and, even more, as the One Crucified for us. For this reason she relives in her senses various moments of the Passion of Christ.

She sees him appear visibly with his hands bound behind his back; in her ecstasies she experiences the stigmata, felt all the more painfully the less they show outwardly.

In connection with the Passion, the Cross with its spirituality dominates her ecstatic visions; other instruments of the Passion dominate too, such as the crown of thorns, which Rosa is impatient to place on her head, almost snatching it from the hands of the Angels.

The Blood and the spirituality of the Blood are linked in Rosa with the Eucharistic Mystery, devotion to which, and the deepening of which, is one of the supporting elements of her supernatural world. She sees the Host bleed during Mass and therefore sinks deep into adoration.

In the mystical life of Rosa Gattorno, the Third Person of the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, never speaks of himself; he makes himself perceived only in relation to the Father and to the Son. The Spirit draws her to Jesus; he shows her the Face of the Redeemer, making her fall in love with an irresistible attraction and with a strength that is no longer her own.

The charism of our Servant of God is thus steeped beyond measure in the supernatural. God led her to range freely in his world with extraordinary gifts of various kinds: visions, apparitions, frequent conversations with heavenly beings, transverberations of the heart, elevations, the reading of hearts, the gift of prophecy, of healings; exultant victories over demonic assaults and infestations.

After contemplating the Trinitarian Mystery, Rosa Gattorno enters into conversation with other persons of the heavenly world, beginning with the Most Holy Virgin, for whom a wholly special place is reserved in her spirituality, as Mother, Teacher, guide, sister.

The other persons who converse with her range from the Angelic world (Michael, the Guardian Angel) to Saint Joseph; from Saint Anne to Saint Francis of Assisi and the Venerable Bernardo Clausi.

Faced with this overflowing invasion of the supernatural, the reader of these pages may, at first impact, be seized by bewilderment; he may think he is dreaming, or that he finds himself in a state of prolonged apnea.

Reason, a prisoner of itself, easily gives itself over to its unyielding incredulity and is always ready to put forward its “ifs” and its “buts.”

But in the case of Rosa Gattorno the “ifs” and “buts” have already been at work all too much, holding back the cause of canonization from 1932 to 1979 under the shadow of the suspicion of abnormality.

But now science too has pronounced on the state of normality of the Servant of God, fully recognized by men of science. For us, therefore, nothing remains but to bow, to admire and to repeat: Digitus Dei est hic! (Ex 8:15).

Repeat it yourself as well, dear reader, because there is no other reasonable explanation. You are invited to do so also by the success of the Work of Rosa Gattorno: 268 religious houses, scattered throughout the world; about 2000 religious.

The mystic seems – and in fact is – an alienated woman. Of herself she does not belong, except through natural ties, to this world. The mystic belongs to another sphere, that of the Divine, and lives in it, permeated by Him, God himself. But when she moves upon the earth, she moves in the most perfect normality, because into her actions too, here on earth, there pours the invasion of the divine which she bears within herself.

Dear reader, take the book in your hands; breathe this mystical atmosphere. You are being offered a work of rare spiritual workmanship.

The spiritual profile of the Servant of God unfolds in chapters which bring out, even through their titles alone, the salient points of the spiritual richness of an exceptional soul.

Let yourself be drawn into the unfathomable depths of the love of God.

PIETRO Card. PALAZZINI.

It is the task of the Institute to guard the charism by opening itself to the Giver of the “gift,” so as to become ever more itself in the Church and to proclaim the gift to all those to whom its mission is addressed, and particularly to the other Members of the Family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate.

To do this, paying attention to the events of God as Jesus inculcated in his teaching, is to guarantee the “gift” itself the right climate for a deeper understanding and a wider diffusion of it.

The Institute has perceived, particularly in this last decade, that the Lord was communicating to it, through persons chosen by him, a new message on the vitality of the charism.

Listening to this message and the consequent welcoming of these persons, and the support to be given in bringing about the new forms of life – expressions of the one charism of the Daughters of St. Anne in the Church – brought to maturity the idea of carrying out a study in order to offer the members of the Family all the elements of the charism and spirituality of the Foundress in an overall view.

1. ITINERARY FOR THE PREPARATION OF A TEXT ON THE CHARISM AND SPIRITUALITY.

Prompted precisely by the flowering of the new forms of life of the charism, the General Council began, in 1989, to draw up the outline of a possible text of spiritual doctrine of the Daughters of St. Anne and of the other Members aggregated and associated with the Institute.

This outline was presented for the first time at the eighteenth General Chapter (1990), to be examined and enriched by the contributions of the Capitulars.

Once the Chapter itself had recognized the value and the need of having a single text offering an overall view of the charism and spirituality of the Family, two phases of work were carried out in the period immediately following the Chapter.

The Assistant for Formation, with the team working for the Charismatic Dynamism of the Institute, took up again the drafting of the second outline (the first, with the suggestions of the 1990 Chapter incorporated) and, at the same time, seeing the need to have the text preceded by an in-depth study of the sources of the Foundress, the Mother with her Council began writing the first volume: “God’s Gift to Rosa Gattorno.”

An integral part of this is the second volume, centered on Rosa’s response to the Gift of God, and the third: “The Treatise of Spiritual Doctrine of the Daughters of St. Anne and of the other Members of the Family of the Holy Mother of Mary Immaculate.”

2. APPROACH TO THE WORK.

In order to make a synthesis of the constitutive elements of the Charism and Spirituality of the Family, it is necessary to examine once more all the writings of the Foundress and of the Co-founder, and the testimonies of those who knew them.

For this reason the study of the charism is carried out on the basis of the Memoirs, for the first volume, and the study of the other two is begun on the basis of the other sources:

- of the Foundress: Memoirs, correspondence, meditations and conferences, various autographs, Rule of the first inspiration;

- of the Co-founder: letters to the Foundress and to her daughters; Rule of 1869; Application of the Common Rule to the Delegate and to the Sisters assigned to the care of the sick.

3. DISTRIBUTION OF THE MATERIAL.

It will consist of three parts:

- Study of the charism of Rosa Gattorno and of the Work which the Lord entrusted to her, on the basis of the Memoirs, transcribed from the autograph ones (1), and of the other documents cited in the text.

  • Study on the spirituality: “The Foundress’s response to the gift which the Lord gave her.”

- “Treatise of Spiritual Doctrine”: the outcome of the values of the charism and spirituality of Rosa Gattorno expressed in her writings, in the Rule of 1869 (in which she sees the gift mirrored), and in the latest text of the Constitutions approved in 1991, a renewed elaboration of the first ones.

4. PURPOSE OF THE FIRST VOLUME.

“GOD’S GIFT TO ROSA GATTORNO”

The text aims to present the fundamental contents of the Charism of Rosa Gattorno and of her daughters and sons in the charism, both consecrated and lay.

It is meant to be a point of reference for all the members of the Family of Saint Anne, so that they may recall the living and dynamic history of the birth of their charismatic Family in the Church and for the world.

It intends to bring out the link between the ways of God’s action in the History of Salvation with the Patriarchs, the Prophets and the Hebrew People in general, and the “Remnant of the poor” in particular, and the way of his interventions in the life and history of Rosa Gattorno.

The text also brings out the bond between the “charism” of the Foundress and the mission of Father Bernardo Maria Clausi and of Father Tornatore in her regard.

It is meant to be a profession of faith in the One and Triune God, contemplated in his merciful love, in Mary, Mother of Jesus and of humanity and our Sister in the charism, in Saint Anne and in all the “Poor” of the Old Testament, in all the Angels and Saints who collaborated with God in the Work entrusted to Rosa Gattorno. It is also a word of thanks to the Foundress for her life and her yes, to Father Tornatore for his dedication and collaboration in the Work of God, and to all those who, in friendship, were a providential support to her (2).

In handing over the completed study to those for whom it is intended, there is a lively hope that their faith may be nourished in the One and Triune God, creator, redeemer, merciful, faithful, protagonist of history. Father, Brother, Spouse and Friend; in Mary, associated with the saving Work of the Son, and Daughter of Saint Anne, conceived Immaculate in her womb; in Saint Anne, sign of the motherhood of God and of the hope rooted in the Covenant which definitively reunites the life of the Father, of Christ Jesus and of the Spirit with the whole of humanity.

The charism of a “foundation” indicates that which animates, informs and gives life to the foundation itself.

In the language of the theology of charisms, a distinction is made between the “charism of the founder”: the gift by which the Spirit has made someone capable of beginning a new form of religious life, and the charism “of the founder”: the way in which he personally lived the gift of grace received.

The dynamism which the Spirit impresses on the founder with the charism, perceived in various forms: inspirations, illuminations, interior locutions, visions..., calls forth a response.

It is precisely in the response that the style of life takes shape: the spirituality (1).

1. A CHARISM IS A GIFT OF THE SPIRIT.

A charism is a gift, a light, a prophecy, a strength, and so many other gratuitous graces of God.

The Holy Spirit sanctifies the Church, “distributing to each one his own gifts as He pleases” (1 Cor 12:11).

He also distributes special graces among the faithful, by which He makes them fit and ready to undertake various works and offices, useful for the renewal and greater expansion of the Church (LG 12).

The Apostle Paul attests that “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good...” (1 Cor 12:7).

In the New Testament the word “charism” never indicates a gift made by one man to another, but always a gift of God, which directly or indirectly is to be considered in relation to Christ and to the action of the Spirit.

Moreover, it is found that charisms are gifts communicated by the Spirit to individual persons, while the Second Vatican Council also speaks of collective charisms, among which the charisms of the founders of the institutes of consecrated life stand out (2).

2. THE CHARISM OF FOUNDERS.

A founder or a foundress is a charismatic person. He or she is a person who has had an evangelical illumination so strong and persuasive as to feel moved to leave everything in order to follow Christ, along the line revealed to the heart by the Spirit.

The particular assistance of the Spirit shapes the person of the charismatic and leads that person in the life of his or her personal holiness. The personal charismatic grace therefore creates, in the mind and heart of the one who receives it, a spirit of its own, a character of its own, that is, a particular way of feeling, thinking, judging, willing, responding and acting, in relation to God’s today, for the building up of the Church and the service of the brethren (3).

It is God himself who, in his Spirit, takes the initiative, making himself present in the life of a man or a woman whom he calls to a particular mission.

The life of the person who bears the “gift” is marked by the power of the Spirit; it unfolds under his guidance, in full docility to his impulses and to interior motions.

The intervention of the Spirit in the many and different phases of a foundation is always present. It manifests itself through extraordinary phenomena such as visions, locutions or special illuminations of the mind, so that one may speak of revelations; or in the attainment of a gradual interior certainty of the kind found in mystical experience; and also through the mediation of persons, or occasioned by the reading of particular circumstances.

The person’s docility to the Spirit allows God to bring to fulfillment, in that person and with that person, his plan in the Church.

Rather than making choices of his or her own, with a more or less explicit deliberation towards the foundation in its fundamental phases, the person is moved by the Spirit.

There is no discursive deliberation, but docility to an impulse. It is therefore a gratuitous intervention in which the free initiative of God appears (4).

With regard to the direct and mystical intervention of the Spirit in the life of Rosa Gattorno, and to that which reached her through mediations, there exists a rich documentation which allows us to grasp well the convergence of the two forms of God’s communication. In the present Constitutions of the Daughters of St. Anne, too, this link is evident: “... the Congregation presents itself to the world as a sign of expectation and of gift, with that attitude of poverty which Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne, expressed in the Magnificat; which Christ, Servant of Yahweh, lived in his earthly life and exalted in the Beatitudes; and which Mother Rosa Gattorno, under the motion of the Spirit, intuited and, with the help of Father Tornatore, made her own...” (Const. art. 3).

The harmony between what the charismatic experiences in solitude with his God and what the same God manifests to him through other persons sent for a mission on behalf of his own “Gift” determines the docility to give the “Gift” concrete form in the originality willed by Providence.

3. PERSONAL TRANSFORMATION AND CHARISM.

The specific inspiration to found an Institute comes, first of all, after the person has been prepared through trial and has grown in union with God, particularly in the exercise of charity.

It presupposes a work of availability and docility to all the charismatic elements which gradually anticipate the foundational “gift.”

If it is true that the charism makes people “fit and ready to undertake various works and offices” (LG 12), this means that it creates in the founder the need to live personally the mission entrusted to him, even before communicating it; indeed, in order to be able to communicate it.

The Spirit takes possession of the person he has chosen to begin the foundation, accompanying that person throughout life: he prepares her, calls her by directly revealing to her the mission she must carry out, consecrates her and leads her to the accomplishment of the task for which she is sent.

The person, for her part, lets herself be permeated by the action of the Spirit, placing herself fully and actively at his disposal, cooperating with him in the realization of her own vocation.

The certainty of being called and sent by God makes her secure in the face of every adversity and trusting in him who has chosen her (5).

The originality of each call and the way of giving it concrete form therefore always come from the Spirit, who through the availability of his creatures goes on renewing the Church.

4. THE SPIRIT CONFORMS THE FOUNDRESS TO CHRIST.

The Spirit sent by the Father and by Jesus is alive and at work in the life of the charismatic in order to reproduce in him the features of Christ according to a particular mystery of his infinite reality.

The person is called, through the charism received, to begin a new path of holiness, to show forth one particular aspect of the infinite mystery of Christ, and is called to do so first of all with her own life, placing herself in the forefront of the following of Christ (6).

The Spirit sanctifies the person, enlightens her, and becomes for her the interpreter and exegete of the teaching of Christ.

This is not a slow, meditative, scholastic process of knowledge, but a rapid and intuitive one, as though by a particular instinct which he communicates to her.

The testimony of Rosa Gattorno about the dynamism of the Spirit in her life leads into an immediate understanding of the Church’s doctrine in this area:

“He, my Love, comes, instructs me as Teacher, furnishes me with most sublime knowledge, sustains me in certain struggles”;

“... my Good helps me, directs me, comforts me, gives me life”;

“... I see that there is a most powerful Spirit who rules and governs me” (M. 1.1, p. 107; 4.1, p. 4).

She, like other founders, was not always clear about the motivations that led her to the contemplation, meditation, identification and radiation of that aspect of the mystery of Christ. She came to it through mystical experience, in which the Spirit unveiled it to her in relation to the Trinity and to Mary, and progressively to Saint Anne, Mother of Mary Immaculate, surpassing all human reasoning and foresight.

Often none of those who surround founders are able to understand the newness of life of which they are the bearers. The charismatic person finds herself alone on the new path to be traveled.

What is lived precedes the systematic doctrinal exposition. The Rule may be written at a later moment, though not necessarily.

What matters most is that the evangelical experience asked of her by the Spirit should have been manifested in her life and mission.

The charism may be formulated by another person endowed with an indirect intuition, who becomes a “collaborator” or “Co-founder” of the work which the charismatic is called to accomplish under the direct action of the Spirit (7).

5. THE FOUNDRESS, PROPHET OF HER TIME.

The foundress penetrates history and events with her contemplative gaze, judges situations in the light of God’s promises and commits herself, with her docility to the action of the Spirit, to anticipating in time and space the mystery of Christ contemplated and loved as the One who is, and who comes to recapitulate all Creation in Himself.

Her charismatic richness, radiating outward, passes to other persons who are drawn in by the same Spirit.

The foundress manifests her life to her disciples through her writings and the Rule, in which she sees mirrored her “charism,” which, being of divine origin, infinitely surpasses her. One cannot grasp all the fullness of the infinite and inscrutable Life of the Spirit, which by its nature surpasses all human understanding (8).

The foundress is a charismatic who submits her “gift” to the discernment of the Church. She awaits its definitive recognition, while she herself is becoming the “gift” she bears. She becomes for her disciples a model to follow.

Rosa Gattorno is for us the model of incarnation, who in her life and in her teachings reproduces Christ in the mystery of his poverty. The clear reference on this point is found in the Constitutions already cited (9).

What the foundress hands on to her daughters and sons is the great passion that animated her, the underlying inspiration, her way of looking at the history of Salvation, of encountering Christ and the Trinity, Mary and Saint Anne and, consequently, her way of looking at the world.

All this, left as an inheritance, contributes decisively to forging “the character and the features” of those who share in the charism as members created to form one and the same Family in the Church (10).

The biblical horizon of vocation and the light that comes from the Magisterium of the Church on this theme allow us to situate in its proper place the vocation of Rosa Gattorno within the universal plan of salvation.

1. GOD’S INITIATIVE.

The admirable initiative of the Creator towards man reveals to us, in all vocations, in the Church and in the world, the nature of God, who in his being Love creates, chooses, calls, reveals “man to man,” and guides him from stage to stage up to the final and indispensable experience of total and definitive surrender to Him who created him by calling him into existence (cf. LG 2).

God is the One who calls and chooses whom he wills. Paul underlines this divine initiative in the Letter to the Romans (9:11-13), citing the election of Jacob in preference to Esau: “When they did not yet exist and had not yet done anything, either good or evil, God said to Rebecca: the elder shall serve the younger.” This shows that God has his own plan in choosing men.

His choice does not depend on their works, but on Him “who calls” (cf. Gal 5:8; 1 Pt 1:15).

God, in his free initiative, chooses man before his birth: “before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you came to the light I had consecrated you; I have appointed you a prophet to the nations” (Jer 1:5).

In the Letter to the Galatians the apostle affirms the same truth with reference to his own vocation: “But when He who chose me from my mother’s womb called me by his grace...” (Gal 1:15).

God not only reaches man with his love by choosing him before his birth, but accompanies him during his existence in every concrete circumstance in which he may find himself: “The Lord said to me: go to those to whom I shall send you and proclaim what I shall command you. Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to protect you” (Jer 1:7-8). He guides him until he fully attains the fullness of life in Christ (Eph 1:3-14).

2. AN ACT OF LOVE.

Vocation is an act of love. God calls man by “name”: “now thus says the Lord who created you..., who formed you...: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you, I have called you by name, you are mine” (Is 43:1). The name corresponds to the unique, unrepeatable image and to the plan of life which He has conceived for each one: “I have called you by name, I have given you a title, though you do not know me” (Is 45:4).

Vocation is a constitutive reality of being. Every man is created to fulfill a mission and to be, in God’s universal plan, that unique and unrepeatable identity: “The desire for God is written in the human heart, because man is created by God and for God; and God never ceases to draw man to himself, and only in God will man find the truth and happiness he never stops searching for...” (1).

In the New Testament the Gospel of Mark presents this dynamism to us in the vocation of the apostles: “Jesus went up the mountain, called to himself those whom He wanted, and they came to Him. He appointed twelve, that they might be with Him and also that He might send them out to preach and that they might have the power to cast out demons” (Mk 3:13-14).

3. DIALOGUE.

Through revelation and personal dialogue with every man, God shows man who he is, what place he occupies and what mission he must carry out in the universal plan of salvation: “From the very circumstance of his origin man is invited to dialogue with God: for he would not exist were he not created by God out of love, and by Him always preserved out of love...” (GS 19).

At every moment He continues to call and to invite this dialogue. To the extent that man responds and makes his relationship with God personal, he understands better all the aspects of his vocational reality: that he has been called to life, to configuration with Christ, to the Church, to holiness, to the glory of heaven (LG 48). (2).

4. CHARISM.

The call to communion with Christ is realized in the Church (LG 2-4). Every Christian, in the Church, occupies his own place and carries out his own mission by means of the particular gift received from the Holy Spirit (LG 4). This gift of the Holy Spirit, called a charism, specifies and makes personal and unrepeatable the identical and radical vocation of all to holiness (LG 7; GS 32). (3).

The different charisms determine the specific vocations in the Church. Every Christian who seeks the truth about himself is committed to discovering and following his own specific vocation, in order to identify and accomplish the good which, in the divine plan, he alone is called to bring about for all men: “Let each one live according to the grace received, placing it at the service of others, as good stewards of God’s manifold grace, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Pt 4:10-11; cf. GS 25).

God wants an upright and generous response, one that embraces the whole of life and existence. Jesus calls this response “perfection” (Mt 5:48), which in the Church’s magisterium is the vocation to holiness (LG 40).

Holiness is realized in different forms, as many as are the specific vocations with which God has adorned the Church and humanity (LG 41). (4).

5. GOD DIALOGUES WITH ROSA.

The vocation of Rosa Gattorno has its place within the universal horizon of the many vocations of God’s plan.

Rosa is called to life, to identification with Christ, to serve her brothers and sisters in the Church and in the world, to holiness and, made like Christ in his death, to go forward to the resurrection strengthened by hope (GS 22).

God, in calling her to life, made of her a human person according to an unmistakable plan.

He continued to dialogue with her discreetly at every moment of her existence and, at the culminating moment of her existential vocation, which is conscious configuration to Christ, He breaks into her life with extraordinary signs and words, revealing to her her mission as foundress in the Church.

The personal relationship which God establishes with her gradually brings to her awareness, so that it becomes her own and not God’s alone, the plan inscribed in her being.

The Father’s design becomes clearer to her through the states of life – marriage, widowhood, religious life – which she is called to live.

The Lord himself breaks into her life with “extraordinary gifts; they are a large part, and an impressive one, of her life. She knew all the temptations, the spiritual desolations: except temptations against chastity. Visions, apparitions, frequent conversations with the Heavenly ones: our Lord, Our Lady, Saint Joseph, Saint Michael, the Guardian Angel, Saint Anne, Saint Francis of Assisi, the Venerable Father Bernardo M. Clausi of the Minims. Stigmata, transverberation of the heart, crown of thorns, elevations and visions of the Mysteries (Most Holy Trinity, Eucharist, Holy Child...). The reading of hearts.

Prophecy.

The gift of healings. Assaults; infestations by demons.” (5).

This initiative of God (6), in the dialogue with Rosa, reveals “Rosa to Rosa,” until the plan of salvation which must pass through her person is brought to fulfillment.

In the history of this divine-human dialogue we find sealed the fundamental aspects of her vocation in the Church. The word addressed to Rosa, spoken in different ways and forms by the Most Holy Trinity, by Jesus, by the Spirit, by Mary, by Anne and by other saints or biblical symbols, contains the plan, the will, the love of God, which must pass through the vocation-mission of Rosa to all men.

Following the stages of God’s manifestations in the mystical life of Rosa Gattorno, the experience of the Trinity takes place about eight years after her radical involvement in the mystery of Christ (2).

There comes about in her what is indispensable for every person. She must reach, as Jesus says, the degree of deep love in order to enjoy the Trinitarian Presence: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (Jn 14:23).

1. ACCESS TO THE TRINITARIAN MYSTERY.

Intimate union with Christ, and Christ Crucified, raised her to the degree of love required by Him so that the Trinity might reveal itself to her.

The description Rosa has left us of her contemplation of the Trinity in 1864 places us before the inaccessible mystery of God, which she, in her human limitation, is unable to express in adequate words.

Although the sense of God’s life in her was developed, nevertheless, before the experience that surpasses all human understanding, she writes only out of obedience to her Good and lets herself be guided by Him:

“Great beyond all telling is the Most Sacred Triad, infinite in God alone, infinite in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Equal in unity, perfect in Trinity. God alone, as one person alone, is seen, and at once in Jesus and in the Holy Spirit, in gazing on the excellence and exquisiteness of these three Persons, in whom one always discerns one person and three, without their being divided! My Love!” (M. 1.2, p. 1).

In an instant she sees and understands the Life of God the Trinity in the depth willed by Himself. This is a knowledge that cannot be reached by human faculties alone. Infused knowledge, in fact, infinitely surpasses every other knowledge and also the spiritual sense of God (3).

In the vision cited Rosa contemplates the Most Holy Trinity in relation to itself.

Theology calls this form the “Trinity in itself,” to distinguish the two modes of being, that of eternity and that of history (4).

Infused knowledge leaves no doubts about the life of God, although He always remains the inaccessible One in his infinite reality.

Consciousness is left changed, shaped by the vision; the object of faith, having been experienced, has opened new horizons. As Saint Paul expresses it fourteen years after his vision of God: “I will go on to the visions of the Lord. I know a man in Christ who (...) was caught up to the third heaven and heard words which no one is permitted to utter” (2 Cor 12:1-4), the experience remains, confirms faith, and impresses on the affections a divine dynamism which drives the person to desire to live and remain in the reality contemplated.

The mystical event:

“in everything, I could say, I saw Paradise and a Triune God! and then all at once one alone, in all his beauty!” (M. 1.1, p. 58), remains, even if trials later come which darken the transcendent horizon of the soul.

2. THE TRINITY DIALOGUES, SHOWING ITS LOVE FOR MAN.

God, whom Jesus revealed in three (5) persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and as God-Love, willed to show his “Face” mystically to Rosa.

With her there conversed the One who in the history of Salvation appears as a reality both near and transcendent, the one divinity, who lets himself be glimpsed as God the Trinity in the Old Testament: “the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Gen 1:2); “Behold, I send my angel before you” (Ex 23:20); “so shall it be with the word that goes forth from my mouth” (Is 55:11); and who reveals himself as such, in the fullness of time, in the Son and through the Son.

This same God was pleased to manifest to Rosa his infinite love for man and his action directed to saving him.

His initiative impresses on her an inexhaustible dynamism which involves her totally:

“Great Mystery. Oh! could I but obtain to make you known by the whole world. You (if one may say so) are mad with love for man, and he? Alas! A Voice that says to me: Yes, I love him greatly, but I am not loved in return. In saying this to me, it drew so near that I felt myself caught up. Oh! Sanctifying Spirit, Divine Essence, ever ready to pour yourself into the ungrateful hearts of men, how so precious a nectar breathes forth, were man to come to taste but a single drop of it. Oh! sweetness without equal. Oh! whoever comes to taste and possess this divine essence, surely all that is earthly serves him only for loathing; his intellect opened by divine power, he communicates with his immortal being and, in that infinite Ocean of infinite greatness, understands all, is made blessed and delights in love. Oh! how infinite you are in your power, despotic, absolute, and then Father and beloved Spouse of hearts. Oh! strength of loving souls and of whoever lives in you and for you” (M. 1.2, p. 1 ff.).

In the mystical embrace, in an instant, she gathers her spiritual faculties in Him, and of each divine Person she contemplates the love, the sanctifying action, the sweetness, the gift of understanding which allows her to communicate with God, in whom the infinite greatness, power and divine lordship is in harmony with his benevolence as Father and beloved Spouse of hearts.

On the same horizon she sees the reality that is opposed to the infinite love of God: ungrateful man.

Thus there emerges ever more clearly, in her vocation, the special love for sinful man.

3. THE DIALOGUE OF THE TRINITY IN THE EUCHARIST.

Attentive, sincere, deep participation in the Eucharist nourishes Rosa’s life, to the point of making her live immersed in the mystery of Christ.

The knowledge of the mystery of Christ’s offering, which is an oblation acceptable to the Trinity, becomes for Rosa an experience. It is the Father himself who grants her the gift of crossing the threshold of the Trinitarian meaning of the Eucharist in order to enter into the Presence of the Trinity.

The Eucharist, in an instant of infused contemplation, becomes intimate union with Jesus, with whom she offers herself to the Father, the presence of a Light and the presence of the Father revealed by the Voice of the Spirit (6):

“While I was hearing Mass and offering to the Eternal Father the Sacrifice of the altar, a most vivid light appeared to me, together with a Voice that said to me: ‘This sacrifice of yours, together with his Beloved Son, is very pleasing to God, but it would please him greatly if you offered yourself as a victim in all the Sacrifices that are celebrated on the altars of the whole Catholic world...’” (M. 1.1, p. 123 ff.).

It is evident that she shares in the Trinitarian action of the Eucharistic Mystery: the Father requires the offering, the Son out of love and in love offers himself, the Spirit pours out his love and makes Rosa a sharer in the life of Christ and in his mission: she must offer herself on all the altars for the glory of God and for the ransom of sinners.

4. GOD THE TRINITY, WHO DWELLS IN HER, SPEAKS.

God, in dialogue with Rosa, manifesting his life in different ways and forms, grants her the gift of experiencing him as present, dynamically at work in her inner life.

The revelation of Jesus about the Trinitarian presence in us: “I in them and you in me, that they may be perfect in unity and the world may know that you sent me and have loved them as you have loved me” (Jn 17:23), finds a true attestation in Rosa’s experience.

It is a true, real Presence (7), that of which she speaks to us:

“...I always find myself in the presence of God... There are times when I truly feel certain words come out of my mouth in answer to the affairs of his Work, and so I never think about what I must say, because my love speaks for me... Words come out that are certainly not mine, but His, who acts and speaks in me. I would say that it is a rest for me, because in Him I remain, tasting his delights” (M. 1.1, p. 149 f.).

It is a Presence that envelops her and draws her towards her innermost center:

“Now I think of my Good who is in my breast. Oh! Love, and when I think of this... I spend stretches of time not remembering that I am alive... absorbed for hours...” (M. 1.1, p. 98).

Many times the Divine Presence is felt as an unquenchable fire that consumes and devours her:

“...in my room, with arms outstretched on the ground, I was praying to my God, the fire was devouring me. Yes, my Love, consume me...” (M. 1.1, p. 160).

She lives the unspeakable experience of the Trinitarian “indwelling.” Indeed, what she experiences is not only a verifying of the fruits of God’s action in her:

“By the grace of God I became aware that all earthly affections were fading away.” (M. 1.1, p. 1), but the welcoming of a Presence and living in It: “as you, Father, are in me and I in you, may they also be one in us...” (Jn 17:21).

The mystical relationship of the Father with Rosa begins in the first stage of her conversion and radical dedication to Christ.

The Father communicates with her through words and symbols which can be interpreted in the light of those he used in the Old and New Testaments.

1. THE FATHER AND THE VOCATION TO MARTYRDOM.

The Father therefore enlightens her gradually, unveiling her vocation to her with words and symbols throughout her life.

The language of these signs points to the redemptive dimension of the Economy of Salvation and to Rosa’s eschatological destiny.

The Father’s initiative creates in her a filial trust and openness which makes her dare to ask for what is impossible by human standards and which might even be considered superfluous in the relationship with him. Her description of the dynamism of the request is surprising:

“...if my Good delayed in letting me see them (cf. M. 1.1, p. 5) (1)... I at once had recourse to the Eternal Father that he might grant me to see them, and he granted it. Now another thing is added, which I see resting upon them, now a palm, now a very beautiful crown. Oh! how beautiful it is!” (M. 1.1, p. 6).

Her experience is the testimony of a style of relationship that reaches the limit of simplicity and trust in Him.

Her relationship is also the fabric into which the action of the Father is woven, an action which, outside the perspective of his tender love, might appear to be too indulgent towards Rosa’s claim.

But it is not so. Beyond the importance of the symbols “palm” and “crown,” which evoke martyrdom and final victory (2), there is the Father’s dynamism towards Rosa: a love which appears all the greater in that it joins the extremes in God: the Eternal One and the “Beloved Father of hearts,” who condescends to her desires.

The Word of Jesus: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God” (Jn 16:27), becomes Rosa’s personal relationship with the Father, lived in the most absolute simplicity.

2. THE FATHER SHOWS HIS “FACE.”

Rosa certainly sought the “Face” of God at so many moments of her prayer, but when the Father manifests to her the “light of His Face” she is filled with his Presence.

The symbol, “smiling Face,” sends us to seek its religious meaning in the Bible.

In the history of Salvation, the search for the “Face of God” is an experience of the Old and New Testaments laden with theological content.

The shining of the Face of God is the revelation of his grace and benevolence (cf. Num 6:25). That is why the just, those who trust in Him, the exiles who remember Him again in the time of trial, pray saying: “who will show us what is good? Let the light of your Face shine upon us, O Lord” (Ps 4:7).

The search for the Face of God, on the part of the devout Israelite or of the Christian, is accompanied by the awareness of being sought and reached by God himself: “I in justice shall behold your Face. On waking I shall be satisfied with your Presence” (Ps 17:15). (3).

The biblical horizon is therefore the theological place whose perspective allows us to understand the mystical experience described by Rosa Gattorno:

“I saw my Eternal Father with a smiling face; he was pointing out to me a vacant place, and then Mary with my Child Jesus in her arms, in the act of handing him to me, and near me there seemed to be another person. My dear Eternal Father made me understand many things, but commanding me not to write them. I will only say that at the last he told me that he would protect me in a particular way in the wars I must sustain, as in those in which we are at present, and not to doubt anything...” (M. 1.1, pp. 39-40).

The Face of the Father, turned towards Rosa, conveys the intensity of his glory in the light that symbolically radiates from his smile (biblically: glory, joy), which enlightens and consoles her.

With this light in her soul, her intellect sees clearly that the Face of the Father becomes ever more present to her in the glorious Face of the Crucified Son, the Beloved, the Guide, the Well-Beloved: “For God, who said: Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts, to make resplendent the knowledge of the divine glory that shines on the Face of Christ” (2 Cor 4:6).

3. THE RIGHT HAND OF THE FATHER.

The dialogue of the Father in the Son is revealed in the permanent dimension of Rosa’s vocation, but there is no lack in her life, as can be seen, of significant experiences of the immediate intervention of the Father.

One, among the other divine prerogatives through which the Father reveals himself, is his Power.

The Bible, and above all the psalms, are interwoven with the religious experience of the Power of God, of his interventions which free, protect and save.

The Power of God is symbolized by the “right hand” of God: “Show me the wonders of your love: you who save from their enemies those who entrust themselves to your right hand” (Ps 17:7).

In the symbol of the right hand, infinitely transcending the symbol itself, which nonetheless announces his Presence, the Father shows his Omnipotence to Rosa:

“...I remained in the presence of the Eternal Father; he was stretching out his right hand to me; it was so resplendent that I cannot express it...” (M. 1.1, p. 58).

Her radical humility, the awareness of her littleness, the feeling of being nothing under the weight of uncommon trials, give her the clear conviction, at the moment of victory, that the one protecting her is God the Father. This is how she expresses herself after a long trial and terrible temptations:

“...his most powerful right hand raises me up, sustains me and always makes me carry off the victory” (M. 1.1, p. 75).

Her expression could be regarded as an echo of the canticle of Mary, which sprang from the recognition of the intervention of God’s mercy and power in her life: “...he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid..., he has shown the strength of his arm, he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their heart” (Lk 1:48-51).

And it finds another parallel in the broad religious experience of Israel, sung in various psalms, in which Almighty God is acknowledged, praised, adored and thanked in terms which symbolize his Presence by the “right hand”: “...with your right hand you have been my support, multiplying your kindness upon me”; “...your right hand is full of justice...”; “...the right hand of the Lord has done wonders” (Ps 18:36; 48:11; 118:16). (5).

Akin to what is exalted in the Psalms is also the mystical experience which Rosa has on October 13, 1869:

“...I made the Holy Exercises; from the very first day, the Eternal Father, ...in my cell, I was in contemplation, ...stretched out his right hand to me and gave me infinite graces. Oh! my Love! Teaching me to distinguish well the true spirit from the false, he gave me very great consolations. Oh! my God!” (M. 1.1, p. 86).

In his immense mercy, the Father, giving Rosa a rich share in his divine life, through religious contents similar to those he had used with the biblical figures most open and faithful to Him, allows the spiritual profile of this daughter of his to be identified without any doubt.

4. THE ETERNAL FATHER AND THE JUDGMENT.

In the details of God’s dialogue with Rosa one truth stands out: He entrusts sinners in a particular way to her care.

The vision which the Father offers her of his judgment on a soul that presents itself before Him after death leaves a deep mark on her life, and certainly spurs her to pray and to offer herself with greater dedication and generosity for the salvation of sinners.

This is how she expresses herself, describing what she saw after a first moment of supplication:

“Oh! my Eternal Father, when will you grant me the grace of letting me die a martyr for the faith? What can I do so that the whole world may love you? Oh! Love, consume me with your divine fire. I saw in a rapture the soul when it stands before the throne of God the Judge, in the act of condemning it. Oh! what a horrible state, what shrieking, what torment. I was left trembling so! when I came to myself I did not dare to raise my eyes or say a word to my Beloved. It seemed to me that I was the one deserving such a condemnation...” (M. 1.1, p. 68).

She understands in an instant the desperate state in which those who refuse grace in the present life come to find themselves.

The refusal of God is a radical possibility of human freedom, which has as its consequence the loss of charity and the privation of sanctifying grace. If it is not redeemed by repentance and God’s forgiveness, it causes exclusion from the Kingdom of Christ and eternal death.

Judgment on persons belongs exclusively to the justice and mercy of God (6).

These truths, founded on Sacred Scripture, taught by tradition in the Catholic Church and experienced mystically, remain painfully impressed on the heart of Rosa, who offers herself with penance and supplications to the Father to obtain the conversion of sinners (7).

5. THE ETERNAL FATHER AND PROVIDENCE.

Towards the last years of her life, reflecting with a retrospective gaze on the bright and dark events she had lived through, Rosa recognizes in everything the guiding thread of Providence (8). She now finds the imprint, in her human and historical fabric, of the truth revealed for centuries: “God does not abandon to itself the creature He has created. He does not only call it to life and to a vocation; he preserves it at every instant of its existence.” (9).

Certainly for her, who recognizes these interventions of God, life is complete dependence, a source of wisdom and freedom, of joy and trust (cf. Wis 11:24-26).

This is how she describes to us one of the many moments in which she receives an abundant providence:

“I was greatly distressed, some days ago, because I lacked the money to pay a bill... My God, what providence! After having prayed much, and the prayer being ended, a few hours later a lady came and brought me all that I needed, telling me she had been sent by a person...; however much I did to learn who had sent her, she would tell me nothing, repeating to me: this person is unknown, pray, and she left me... I was so overwhelmed; at once I hurried to the chapel to thank my God for the providence he deigned to send me” (M. 1.1, p. 71 f.).

She discovers the power of prayer, which brings about the Father’s response. The words of Jesus: “Do not be anxious, then, saying: what shall we eat? what shall we drink? what shall we wear... For your heavenly Father knows that you need them. Seek first the Kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be given you besides” (Mt 6:31-33), are abundantly confirmed for her by the Father:

“...Take comfort, for you shall have all that you ask of me.” These are words which he addresses to her in a moment of prayer:

“While I was lying face down, stretched out on the ground, with my forehead resting on the floor, my arms extended in the form of a cross, the Eternal Father, joy of my soul, said to me: take comfort, for you shall have all that you ask of me” (M. 1.1, p. 78).

The providence she receives is for the work which God himself has entrusted to her, in a particular way to console and soothe the suffering of the poor (10).

Among all the providential signs, one expresses the Father’s special love for the sick:

“...he charged me to give them a small cloth (to dear ones during the plague)... anointed with the oil... blessed by the Eternal Father, and to assure them that nothing would happen to them; and so indeed it came about” (M. 1.1, p. 40).

The gift of the blessed oil reserved for Christmas Eve, when God’s lowering of himself to heal the wounds of humanity and restore to it hope and salvation reaches the utmost sharing in our history, undoubtedly affirms the harmony between the divine reality, the symbols that represent it and the aspect of the mystery of Christ which Rosa must embody in the Church:

“It is two years since..., on the eve of the birth of the Child Jesus, the Eternal Father himself taught me to prepare a certain oil which he blesses for the sick. What great healings I have seen worked and, if they are not healed, it quenches the pain and gives them peace and tranquility of soul to die well” (M. 1.1, p. 69).

The experience described lets us glimpse that the Father sends her to the sick; for this reason he transmits to her his power veiled in matter – a sign which in the Old Testament was regarded as a medicine to relieve pain or restore health to the sick, and in the New is also a symbol of the healing power and of the divine victory in every human infirmity: “Is anyone sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, after anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer made with faith will save the sick person: the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins they will be forgiven him” (Jas 5:14-15).

Through her responsibility towards those she loves, Rosa shares in the divine activity of the Creator, who loves and cares for every creature, however small.

The sublime will of the Father to identify Rosa with his Beloved Son is manifested to her, in a special way, through her mystical experience with Jesus Crucified. In her life she does not live only the historical memory of the Crucified One, but dialogue with the glorious Jesus, who lets himself be experienced by her in the mystery of the crucifixion.

It is an encounter of love with him, from which she learns to give meaning not only to the joys and gifts she receives, but also to the pain of humanity and to her own sufferings. From Jesus she learns to love suffering as a sharing in his passion and ignominious death, the perfect sacrifice and the new and Eternal Covenant (1).

1. THE BLOOD OF THE REDEEMER.

As in the Old Testament the Covenant between God and his people was founded on the sacrifice of immolated animals, and their blood sprinkled on the defiled purified them, so the new Covenant is founded on the blood of Christ. In Him, indeed, who through an eternal spirit offered himself without blemish to God, our conscience is purified from dead works, to serve him in holiness and justice (cf. Heb 9:14).

Rosa lives the mystical experience of this mystery of the economy of salvation. Several times she sees in vision the ransom of her sins:

“...For a long time... he showed me two books... In them certain names were written and then Saints; at the end there was my name written large and then Saint, written distinctly; in the other, which was thick, there were my sins; more than half of it was written on, and I saw them all canceled with the Blood of my Dear Redeemer...” (M. 1.1, p. 5).

The “precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without defect and without fault” (1 Pt 1:18 f.), is the symbol of redemption (cf. Mt 26:28). The beginning of Rosa’s conversion is marked by this symbolic presence of the Blood of Christ. She is purified by the blood so as to deserve to be among those who “have washed their robes, making them white in the blood of the Lamb, stand before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his sanctuary” (Rev 7:14 f.).

Her life passes through the experience of the shedding of blood and remains as a precious testimony to the immeasurable value of the “blood” of Christ in the work of redemption (2).

2. IDENTIFICATION WITH CHRIST CRUCIFIED BRINGS FORTH PEACE AND SWEETNESS.

The spirituality of the Cross is an evident feature of Rosa’s life. The promise of Christ: “when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself” (Jn 12:32) is fulfilled in her. The life of Christ is poured out in her; particularly during Communion she feels herself conformed to Him. She is taken up into the mysteries of his life, made like Him in death and in the blessedness that comes from his resurrection:

“Oh! dear Jesus! Yes, let us grow fond of Calvary, and in suffering we shall see its delights; as we draw near to the object that is loved, all suffering becomes a balm that one longs for. In the caresses he gave me he often presented me with something of his gifts, such as that of meditation, and this after Holy Communion. Clasped to my Good (which was more a contemplation than meditation), because I would place myself in a wound and stay there for hours and was not aware of being alive” (M. 1.1, p. 5).

Tribulations associate her with the sufferings of Christ, but she also receives the fruits of the Resurrection (3).

The particular details of the mysteries of Christ’s life which she is given to contemplate send her back to the totality of the mystery: He, alive and present in her person and in her history. For him she bears every temptation and yearns to possess every form of pain suffered by him. This is how she expresses herself in the following text:

“Now I see... a crown of thorns which I rejoiced to possess. Oh! poor sinner! Such was my desire for the crown of thorns that I would hide myself in it in Holy Meditation, and I set Thursday as the day to stay and meditate on it. After Most Holy Communion, one day I saw two Angels approach with a crown of thorns in their hands, which resembled that of my Beloved; it had one very long thorn; they were drawing near to place it on my head, and I was all eagerness to feel it pressed down on my head, although the thorns were very sharp. The desire to suffer was great, the pleasure was immense. Oh! how happy I would have been if they had left it with me forever. But no, I only obtained permission to wear one like it on the night of Thursday and Friday. The enemy began to beat me and gave me so hard a blow right in the middle of the forehead, where I had the thorns of the crown, that one of them went in” (M. 1.1, pp. 6-7).

3. VARIOUS ASPECTS OF THE SUFFERING CHRIST.

The presence of Jesus Christ in the different aspects of his paschal mystery urges her to be configured to Him in poverty, in humility and in voluntary powerlessness. The signs through which Jesus reveals to her the mysteries of his life strengthen her spiritually: she feels stronger in suffering, more aware of the richness of the gifts she receives, more conscious of her littleness, but also more intimately united to Jesus who lives in her.

She introduces us to this vision of her life in Christ with her memoirs:

“One day I was sitting in the country, in an open space, on the ground; I had a small cushion under me, and I was reciting the office of the Most Blessed Virgin. Oh! what did I see close to me: my Jesus bound, with his hands behind him.”

“Oh! what I felt! Oh! my Love, you alone could say what these visits of yours produced in me. Strength again for suffering, resignation to your divine Will. Oh! my Love! When the recitation of the office was ended I thanked my Good for so great a favor to a wretched sinner... but it is not I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me” (M. 1.1, pp. 11-12).

It is Jesus, the living and permanent presence in the Church: “I am with you always, until the end of the world” (Mt 28:20), who unveils himself to her.

This Presence of the living, glorious Christ, in whom all the earlier moments of his life are summed up, from the incarnation to his death, breaks in upon her. The glorious presence of Jesus opens her, in faith, to personal encounter with Him and to the experience of uninterrupted communion. No wonder, then, that he lets himself be experienced with attitudes and gestures that correspond to his innermost being (4), just as Rosa describes:

“Oh! what I felt on seeing Jesus weep. On coming back to myself, I found myself so cast down, as if I had wept bitterly, and an inner pain, for as much as it was given me truly to see, remained with me.

So deep was my pain that for a long time I could not stop having a kind of sobbing; the pain was strong beyond all telling...” (M. 1.1, p. 36).

4. THE WOUNDS OF JESUS CRUCIFIED.

The aspects of the mystery of Christ most evident in the mysticism of Mother Rosa are Love, the constant and glorious Presence (5), the self-emptying: “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil 2:8).

Jesus makes himself visible to her in the inseparable reality: love-cross. Her soul is pierced by the great mystery of our salvation: “He was put to death for our sins and was raised for our justification” (Rom 4:25).

The Love of Christ for the Church: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her” (Eph 5:25), becomes, in her mystical experience, an event that transforms and sanctifies her.

Her love, in fact, ever more total and exclusive, for her Crucified Good is evident in what she writes:

“As I was about to begin the meditation, I found myself before the wound of the right foot of my Good, dripping with blood. Oh! what I felt; I remained absorbed in him, I cannot say for how long! I saw nothing then, I only felt a strong pain, and it seemed to me so intense that I could not bear it. Oh! my Love! what did I not feel, afterwards, when I came back to myself! you alone could tell it” (M. 1.1, p. 35).

The union which holds her bound to Him sharpens her hearing to listen to his Voice: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow me” (Lk 9:23). And in the harmony between the divine Presence that imposes itself and her own personal commitment, she is led to experience the love and the pain present in every wound of the Divine Body of the Redeemer and Savior of humanity:

“Caught up again, I find myself close to the Side of my Beloved, and what I felt...”.

“Only when I have afflictions and tribulations do I then feel some relief, because I feel this fire less. Oh! what a thirst I have to suffer; I feel nothing of pain, because the thirst for suffering is without equal! it is sweet to suffer for the beloved!

On the 7th I had something in meditation that caught me up, and I remained as if I were close to the wound of the shoulder. Oh! my Love, afterwards I learned to say: with my tears I will wash this wound and draw out its moisture. Oh! at once a flood of tears came to me and, as if with my very mouth I could draw out that balm, I came to myself and found myself full of strength, whereas before I was worn out by my labors for the sick and the poor whom I went to help; I felt myself almost fainting when I returned to my poor room” (M. 1.1, pp. 41; 58-59).

The visits of Jesus impress indelibly on her heart the datum of faith: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pt 2:21). This is how Rosa speaks of these encounters:

“Crucified Love appears to me and shows me his wounds! A flood of weeping, and I can go on no longer; and so that it would not be noticed I ended, and I do it no more, because it always continues in me. But this is a balm to me in the tribulations in which I find myself” (M. 1.1, p. 121).

With the Apostle who professes: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me” (Gal 2:20), she attests to the presence of Christ in her:

“But I always remained recollected on the point of the wound of the shoulder, and with my mind I would have wished to heal it. And behold, my Good appears to me so wounded, and I said to him: My dear Love, wounded like this, how am I to tend you? Ah! let me take off my skin and lay it on your wound; I cannot bear it, I am dying of pain! And as soon as I had said this, his wound was healed. Oh! my Love, have you accepted this wretched flesh? and he disappeared.

How much strength he gave me. Robust as if I had done nothing; daylight came, and I found myself still in Church, strengthened by my Love, so that I can say: being of my living, because I do not live, but it is my Good who lives for me” (M. 1.1, p. 144).

5. THE WOUNDS OF JESUS ON HER BODY.

Rosa Gattorno speaks several times of her sharing in the pains of the wounds of Christ.

This state of compassion in the soul is aroused by God through supernatural stigmatization, which affects the body. The outward stigmata imply the inward ones, an essential aspect of sharing in the passion of Jesus (6).

In the description she has left us in the Memoirs it is clear that the stigmata are for her a charismatic grace. God grants them to her in ecstasy, during which the signs of the Crucifixion are connected with those of the glory of Christ: consolations, sweetness, love, divine fire, the vision of sublime realities, further locutions:

“I went to climb the Holy Stairs in Rome; I was caught up and remained in my God, so united with my Beloved that I no longer lived. I felt great consolations; I was seized by pain in my hands and feet and heart, and all my veins (on coming to myself) seemed filled with boiling blood; the region of the heart also seemed open; what I felt was such that it cannot be expressed.”

“Having come to myself, I forced myself and went back home, and at once I tried to lie down, in the hope of finding a little relief. But no! my hopes came to nothing. After a little while, the fire increased in me so much that it seemed to consume me. My Love drew near to me and caressed me. The pains in my hands and feet and heart grew, and I seemed to be expiring. I seemed to have a furnace upon me, and I remained in ecstasy a long time; I saw most beautiful things; he told me things I desired to know, he gave me their explanation, he strengthened me with a certain something, so that, when I had come to myself, I felt stronger, and the pains in my feet, hands and heart were less. Thus inebriated I stayed thinking of what I had seen and enjoyed; I remained so a good 2 hours” (M. 1.1, pp. 49-50).

The call to identification with Christ entails for her, besides spiritual crucifixion, bodily crucifixion as well.

Her path of growth to perfection in love and of fruitfulness in mission passes through the radical assimilation of the experience of Jesus, the man who loves and obeys unto death on a cross (Heb 2:10; 5:7-9). (7).

She knows that she has received everything from God and that the sharing in his pain, too, is a free gift to a frail creature such as she considers herself to be:

“In the first days of January 1870 I had very severe pains in my hands and feet and heart; the spasms were terrible; I often had recourse to water to find relief. Oh! what torments, and these never cease for me, because they ease a little by day so that I can work, and then, Oh! my Love!

One day they were so strong that, having shut myself in my room, I looked at my feet; the pains were more cruel. I found in the middle of them a swelling almost two fingers high, and I had to lie down, because the pain was stronger than I. As soon as I lay down I was caught up and enjoyed the most beautiful visions; I received great explanations about what was to be done for his Work, as also about certain ones received years before, and even some from when I was a young girl” (M. 1.1, p. 88).

Of these gifts she speaks to Him with gratitude and a lively sense of humility:

“You have given me hands, feet, side: these are treasures, but I have nothing. I am exceedingly wretched, and you, my Good, who deign to give me so much” (M. 1.1, p. 154).

6. JESUS CRUCIFIED AND THE FOUNDATION.

At a stage of mature configuration to Christ Crucified, in one of her frequent moments of intense prayer, by the same Christ Crucified, in continuity with what she is living, her vocation-mission as foundress in the Church is unveiled to her.

We draw from her Memoirs the essential elements of the dialogue with Jesus, which constitutes the original foundation of the great Work whose dimensions would be unveiled to her in time:

“When it was ended, I felt so beside myself, and I folded everything. Then, taking up my dear Crucifix again, I thanked him. Oh! I clasped him to my breast, my Love! Having said this, behold I was once more caught up in ecstasy, and he himself, I felt it clearly, was dictating a rule to me; thus he said to me: (what he dictated to me was so clear; it seemed that this dictation had a different effect on me) ‘Write at once what I have told you.’ These were the last words and, having come to myself, I did not delay in obeying; I wrote down exactly what he had dictated to me and put them away, well guarded...” (M. 2, pp. 6-7). (8).

Under the direct action of God, who would guide her with jealous love, the Words of her Crucified Good would accompany her until they became fully evident.

Her fears, her perplexity, her doubts are no obstacle for God, who has found in her, up to this point, a response of radical love for Christ. He now requires the same availability for the Work that must arise in the Church with her. This is how she describes this demand of her God:

“...those which I had put away..., began to trouble me, because an inner Voice kept tormenting me, telling me that I must show them, that it was His work; but I drove it away and, to say it better, I did not understand what was wanted. One evening: what do you want, my dear Crucifix? why must I show this writing, what is it to serve for? He answered me: ‘for the Work that I want; great it shall be!’ My God! I set myself to think and understood nothing of it: where is it to be, who is to do this work? I felt so confused; I gave up the thought and set myself to pray, clasped to my dear Crucifix, and a Voice which was certainly His, my Good’s, said to me: ‘from you I want this Work. Take to the Archbishop the writing you have.’ Oh! how my mind was thrown into confusion; another work, how to undertake it? what shame to say this to the Archbishop! Oh! my God, I feel that my strength is not enough to do what you command me; I feel myself dying at the very thought of it, and my children, my mother...” (M. 2, pp. 10-11).

Through the spiritual events of her life Rosa understands that the absolute protagonist of her life is God. To Him, therefore, she turns with trust, certain of having the decisive answers for the accomplishment of the Work itself at the moments when the unfolding of events marks out a direction that goes beyond her.

To her supplication, in one of these dark moments, the Voice clearly answers:

“All that happened is my will; be at peace, everything will be made smooth!...” (M. 2, p. 47).

In the intimacy of the contemplative life, Jesus the Teacher (1), Jesus who reveals to her the Father’s design for her person, is the “wisdom” of Rosa Gattorno’s life. He loves her tenderly, forms her with special love in spiritual growth and goes on showing her her final destiny.

1. CONVERSATION WITH JESUS.

In her first mystical experiences (between 1857 and 1861) Rosa experiences special gifts of the Lord. She attributes to him the gift of knowing how to meditate and above all to contemplate. She understands that for a beginner it would not have been easy to remain for hours in him, as instead happened to her when she fixed herself on one or another wound of the Crucified.

In one of her first mystical experiences she expresses herself thus:

“...I was absorbed and remained as if in conversation with my Jesus; he taught me many things” (M. 1.1, p. 5).

In 1862, in a period of struggle with the evil one, Jesus enlightens her on the discernment of spirits, making her pass through a painful but liberating experience. It is an experience that confirms her regarding the power of Christ over her life and above all his power over the evil one (2), whose harassments she must not fear. He enlightens her on the meaning of certain diabolical actions.

This is how she recounts this phase of liberation:

“...he (the devil) would come out with new inventions, but my Director knew well how to find a way to make me touch with my own hand that nothing would happen at the hour of my death, and so with the rest of what the dragon whispered to me” (M. 1.1, p. 28).

Finding herself alone, she felt ill, but nothing of what the devil whispered to her happened. Once the illness had passed, the Voice of Jesus intervenes:

“...now you will believe that they are all temptations; but was it not enough for you to have seen everything canceled? and he adds still more by way of reproach. Oh, what pains I felt at this! But I kept thinking of the peace of that moment when I was fainting... How sweet it is to die with Jesus...” (M. 1.1, p. 29).

2. THE PRESENCE OF JESUS ON CERTAIN FEAST DAYS.

On certain feast days (3), Jesus grants her lights, spiritual gifts, illustrations which introduce her into future events, known to God alone.

On the yearly feasts of the circumcision of Jesus, besides being filled with gifts and lights, she hears explanations she desires to have about various facts and situations. Jesus strengthens her with his love and introduces her into the divine mysteries with blessed ecstasies:

“I remember that it was the eve of the circumcision; I was on a journey, and all night long I was with Jesus and Mary, who were visibly always near me and were instructing me in what was to happen to me... Oh! what I felt that night! My Love drew near to me... I remained in ecstasy, I saw most beautiful things; he told me things I desired to know, he gave me their explanation, he strengthened me. Thus inebriated I stayed thinking of what I had seen and enjoyed, a good 2 hours” (M. 1.1, pp. 49-50).

As God’s decision about Sodom and Gomorrah is made known to Abraham (cf. Gen 18:16 ff.), so Rosa contemplates God’s judgment on Rome and Paris, so that she may take part in it with prayers, offerings and penances.

Significant and programmatic is the illumination concerning the trial which the Father permits for sinners, which leads her to offer herself as a victim for them and to beg Jesus himself insistently to suspend his chastisements on the cities of Rome and Paris. The description she gives of it underlines the different elements of the economy of salvation (4):

“Another day he showed me how angered His Majesty was, and that there was nothing that could calm him. Mary was praying, and I was terrified at the sight of the utter destruction of two cities, one by fire and the other by war. One, Paris, was fire, and Rome at war! The slaughter was horrible; my God, have mercy; and I offered myself as a victim so that upon me he might (pour out) everything and be calmed. How much I suffered I cannot describe; I was left so stricken that I could not revive. Everything served me for pain, always with the sight of my God before me, in a severe and angered attitude!...” (M. 1.1, pp. 51-52).

The divine horizon of justice and the vision of hardened sinners bring about her offering, an act which configures her to Christ the Victim. But it is evident, in this case, that it is not she who goes before the Master; it is He who guides and forms her in the accomplishment of her vocation-mission in the Father’s plan.

Child, in whom littleness and transcendent greatness stand out.

The Child teaches her how to pray and helps her to live her trials, her sharing in the mystery of redemption in order to save souls:

“...when I saw this I was caught up in him, and I saw the Face of my little Good, who seemed to be teaching me to pray and was giving me other knowledge; a very strong fire remained in me...” (M. 1.1, p. 55).

And on the day of the Nativity of Mary she sees other aspects of the divine reality of Jesus:

“Oh! sweetness. Oh! Love who make me be consumed! On the 8th of September, Oh! my Love, absorbed in him, I saw my little Jesus coming to me, and while I saw this I was telling the angels (5) to cover me, so that Jesus might not see me so deformed. My Love, your charity is without equal! Oh! how many things did I not learn?” (M. 1.1, p. 152).

3. THE MYSTERY OF THE POVERTY OF JESUS.

Called to identify herself with the divine Victim, Christ in the mystery of his poverty, she contemplates various aspects of this reality of his. She sees him small, in the likeness of a Child Jesus, who forms her to value every gesture, however small, and to clothe herself in his littleness:

“All at once, behold my little Jesus, and with him an angel, little too, in the act of adoring him. Now that I am writing I no longer even know how to move the pen. See, he also wanted me to write for whom I have for years been offering my fasts! I am smaller than an insect and so I do the things of little ones, and even these trifles are acceptable to my Good. Monday is for the souls in purgatory; Tuesday for sinners and the dying; Wednesday for Saint Francis of Assisi and Saint Joseph; Thursday I offer to the Eternal Father in honor of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament; Friday for my children, that he may keep them good Christians for me; Saturday in honor of Mary Most Holy; Sunday for Holy Church and the Supreme Pontiff, Cardinals, Bishops. Why, Jesus, does it please you that I write this too? So I said to him, but I received nothing; I only feel a great consolation at having written it, and a fire that consumes me” (M. 1.1, p. 161).

Jesus is an unsurpassable and jealous guide in the most demanding moments of the Foundation:

“I turned to my Good and begged him to tell me how I should conduct myself, and I was instructed how I was to act and speak... My Good had furnished me with his strength...” (M. 1.1, p. 56).

4. YOU SHALL SEE HEARTS.

Infinite Wisdom gives her a share in its Light (6), which penetrates the hearts of men, searches them, shakes them, converts them:

“He let me see into certain hearts and said this to me: every time you need to see them and penetrate them, you shall see them. So too, what you ask of me for the good of the souls who are with you and of whom you have the care, I will give you all of it. So also for what you desire for Priests: the very thing that with prayer you wish me to give them, I will give them. You shall distinguish clearly the good from the bad; I will make you feel an abhorrence whenever they have foul ideas against chastity. At once you shall feel it and be warned of it. Do not doubt, for I shall always be near you; there are many of them... Oh! what pain... I felt. So also for false devout women you shall have special lights to distinguish well...” (M. 1.1, p. 63).

She receives most beautiful instructions on the love which Jesus bears for man, while man responds poorly:

“Oh! my Beloved! Oh! Yes, I see well how much you love creatures, and they respond to you so poorly. You are all love for him! A Voice answered me: yes, I love man immensely; and while it was saying this to me it drew near to me” (M. 1.1, p. 152).

New lights project her towards the future with optimism and hope. She must not fear, because there is One who guides her, sustains her and plans for her:

“At night, behold he came to console me. He showed me what will happen at my death, what they will do with me, how they will dress me, and who will have authority over it; it will be the one who has my final direction, who will live by obedience, but will take care not to command me things which he has not first felt well within himself; the tertiary’s habit will be my habit, and the rest that of Saint Anne” (M. 1.1, p. 164).

With the expert guidance of her Teacher she sees the different aspects of her path in the following of Christ the Poor One. Jesus shows her gradually, walking with her, how to collaborate in the work of redemption.

He forms her for penitent conversion, for engaging in the struggle with the evil one and mastering him by unconditional faith in her Lord, for being a victim of love so as to create the counterweight in the divine justice provoked by our sins, for bringing sinners to salvation.

Union with the Beloved evokes the revelation which God has made of himself to humanity. The Scriptures proclaim that God is Love and that his love makes itself present in the life of every person. Jesus, the Beloved, shares this Love with Rosa and forms her for an intimate and exclusive relationship with himself, modeled on that of the Father for the Chosen People (Is 5:1) and for the Bride of his Beloved Son: “The Love of God was manifested among us in this: God sent his Only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might have life..., in his Beloved Son” (1 Jn 4:9; Eph 1:6; cf. Col 1:13).

1. THE BELOVED OF THE FATHER IS PRESENT IN ROSA’S LIFE.

The same Jesus whom the Gospels present beside Martha and Mary in tears, in the act of supporting the widow of Nain and of absolving the sinful woman, while he weeps over Jerusalem for her children, we find, in the experience described, at Rosa’s side:

“But when they came to such a degree (the tribulations) that I felt myself fainting, behold my Good took everything away from me and I remained in perfect calm.

I had my Beloved near. Oh! what I felt!

Although I no longer saw him, because he had gone, yet I would never have ceased to remain like that, like one who prays, does not pray, I say it better, stays tasting what her Beloved has given her...” (M. 1.1, p. 10).
