In this tasting and contemplating of what Jesus gives her in love, she goes on being identified with Him who died so that she might no longer live for herself, but for Him who died and rose again (cf. 2 Cor 5:14 f.). She experiences, like Saint Paul, that it is not she who lives, but her Beloved who lives in her:

“But it is not I who live, it is my Jesus who lives in me...” (M. 1.1, p. 12).

The call to be configured to Christ Crucified demands of her the price of absolute docility to the will of the Beloved. It entails for her the radical gift of self according to the measure of the gift of the Beloved himself. He, however, supplies her with strength and perseverance in the far from easy process of identification with Him:

“...Temptations came upon me, and the enemy assailed me with new assaults. Such is the combat that I am left without strength, but my Beloved furnishes me with his strength to resist” (M. 1.1, pp. 12-15).

“But I am weak, O my Love, give me a little of your strength to be able to resist everything; when these words were ended, behold I remained in perfect calm, without pains, as one restored and healed!” (M. 1.1, p. 15).

2. GOODNESS AND CHARITY OF THE BELOVED.

The Beloved goes before her and enlightens her in the ways of the Father. He grants her graces, but at the cost of her personal sacrifice. He gives her a share in the Economy of redemption, making her understand that the healing of a person, the conversion of a sinner or the peace of a city are the fruit of a personal oblation associated with the one and unrepeatable oblation of Christ Jesus:

“The goodness and charity of my Beloved made up for all my miseries. He told me that he would heal her (a Superior), but that there was need of the washing – of that wound which she had – with my blood, and so I did, shedding much of it by means of a hard discipline to the point of blood. Again he showed me the chastisement of Rome, and then I said to my Good: ah! for charity’s sake, have mercy on that people; and that, through the prayers of the good souls who were in that city, he might be calmed and forgive, suspending the chastisement.

He showed me the duplicity of hearts and and... Oh! my Love! The Pope! the Pope! dear Pius IX, Oh! how he showed me how much he loved him. He will have nothing... he showed me a thousand other things, but all of them beautiful, which raised me up from the sad dejection in which I found myself. Oh! could I but say what I saw and felt on the day of Corpus Christi. Oh! my Love!” (M. 1.1, p. 53).

Trust in the Beloved makes her overcome the distance that lies between the Infinite and the creature. Through the intimate relationship which the Beloved offers her, making her live in his love, she dares to ask what will become of her life. Having received the answer, she goes on begging him to let her die consumed by his Love:

“My Beloved, will this perhaps be the day on which you will consume me? Oh! no! for at once he showed me that I still had much left to live... I said to him: then, my Good, tell me that by this fire my life will be extinguished. Having come to myself, I went to the hospital, where I found all my happiness, because nothing discouraged me and nothing disgusted me. Cleaning the wounds was the most welcome thing, because it seemed to me that I was doing it to my Dear Jesus. So many times I had to try to distract myself so as not to remain caught up in Him, and to refrain from kissing them, because afterwards I realized that the sick woman spoke of it; so too from sucking them, for fear that it would come to be known; this I had noticed” (M. 1.1, p. 61).

3. THE BELOVED IN TRIBULATIONS.

The choice of the Beloved and of his kingdom does not spare Rosa tribulations and calumnies. The Gospel imperative: “Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” (Jn 12:25) is impressed by the Spirit like a seal on her heart.

The eighth beatitude proclaimed by Matthew: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (5:10)” is like an understanding of love with the Beloved, to remain in Him and enjoy his consolations:

“My inner being rejoices, my soul exults (in tribulations and calumnies) with consolation, and I feel a peace without equal. Oh! my Love! I saw many things in these days, and my Beloved assured me that soon I shall have great consolations.”

“I find myself in the most horrible pains, spiritual ones, which for me are the greatest, because I do not find, I do not see my Beloved, I have not heard his delightful Voice for several days. Alas! what have I done, my Love, being of my living. My Eternal Father, ah, do not abandon me! Come, tell me what I have ever done. Ah! no, a thousand torments, but not these. The others, then, were of a most horrible kind. Alone! Jesus, you know it, I have no one but you, who leave me in this state; I am dying of pain; and behold, my Love is with me. Oh! how many caresses did he not give me! it would take too long to describe them: union, raptures, light to see those who were tormenting me, why they did it, who had moved them to do it!” (M. 1.1, pp. 77; 126).

Rosa’s experience would not have been possible if God himself had not willed, guided and sustained it. She opens her heart to the absolute benevolence of the Beloved, abandons herself in Him, accepts his unlimited demands: she encounters divine love and is filled with graces.

In the Beloved she finds gathered up all the love of the Father and of the Spirit for her. Abiding in the Beloved, who is the perfect response of love to the Father, she enjoys the certainty of being pleasing to Him.

She cannot deny the Beloved what he asks of her:

“My Beloved keeps suggesting to me new sufferings, how I should go about afflicting myself more. I have not one thought that is earthly; I work, I act, because my Good is always with me. It is now 4 days and nights that he has been always visible at my side. I abandon myself wholly in Him. Oh! God with me, who can be against me? the whole world is a nothing, less than a nothing.

I also see that he is not content with the food I take, and I do not understand why; he does not explain himself well, clearly; being ignorant and having no one, what am I to do? for I keep saying to myself: what must I give up? I eat nothing but legumes, a little pasta in soup, and strict abstinence, without dairy foods, nor fruit, because from the age of 25 I made a vow to Mary never to eat it again, especially that of which I was so fond, which one may say was my only food. So what must I give up? Tell me, my Love, what must I give up? perhaps I must do as in that year when you no longer allowed me to eat, which was before you gave me the Holy Rules. Only a little bread every 24 hours. My Love! but speak to me and teach me what I must do.

Having said this, behold he answers me: as you used to do, bread alone, but twice a day; and he assigned me the quantity that would be enough for my sustenance, and to drink, as usual, water. Oh! how sweet that way of living was to me, forgetful of everything; my Love alone made me blessed!” (M. 1.1, p. 112 ff.).

4. THE BELOVED PROTECTS HER FROM THE ENEMY AND FORMS HER FOR THE MYSTERIES OF THE GOD WHO IS PRESENT.

The challenge of the enemy does not weaken her fidelity to the will of the Father or her one longing to be like Jesus and in Jesus. In her words one feels all the strength brought to her by the witness of the Beloved’s life: “...obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil 2:8); “...Jesus said: It is finished. And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit...” (Jn 19:30).

If Jesus died for the life of the Church and of the world, she too is ready to die for the life of the Work of God:

“All at once I feel something drawing near. Oh! it was my Good, Jesus, my Beloved! I felt myself clasped to Him and remained thus absorbed in my Good. I saw a man holding a stiletto in his hand, in the act of wanting to plunge it into my throat... with a furious voice he said to me: ‘withdraw from this work, or else I will kill you’...”.

“It shall never be. Even if I had to undergo all the martyrdoms of this earth, I shall always be your slave and you my Beloved.

A Voice answered me: look at me, how meek I am; and a little lamb appeared to me. It had the wound in its breast, from which blood was flowing: what an impression this sight made on me! It caressed me; its drawing near made me die of love. The fire on the side of the heart was very strong and lasted long, alas. My Love, I am dying. Oh, my dear little Lamb!” (M. 1.1, pp. 147-148).

Associated with her Beloved, she frequently lives the obligatory passage of trial, but the trials of the absence of the Loved One are atrocious.

When the Beloved is present, even if not yet in fullness as in glory, paradise is within her; but she must pass through the painful experience of Him who lived in infinite measure this void between presence and absence, with that density which those who refuse the divine presence are destined to live.

This void, willed and not removed, is the permanent sorrow of the Beloved, and she must taste it in order to offer herself in the name of those who inflict it on him, so that they may come to an adequate knowledge of the reality of God and of man.

The deep personal experience of what the Beloved makes her live transforms her too, and she becomes the Beloved one. Only thus can he ask her to join in his redemptive offering for the salvation of sinners:

“Jesus spoke to me thus: ‘See, my beloved, when you rejected me and fled from my sight, so the cloud in which I was, and I called you several times, and you always turned elsewhere and drove me away, and I abandoned you; you sought me, but you no longer found me. So it is with the damned: they will find me no more!’. Oh! what pains; yes, my Good, it is a cruel torment that I felt. Oh! at the mere thought of it I feel myself shudder...” (M. 1.1, p. 168).

This infused knowledge motivates, beyond every human criterion, her absolute offering for the salvation of sinners.

The profound experience of Rosa Gattorno, based on contemplation, undoubtedly takes priority over the intellectual search for God.

For her the revelation of Jesus: “God is love” (1 Jn 4:8) is not only a mystery of faith to be meditated on; it is above all an experience of love, the welcoming of a Presence dwelling in her being (1).

1. THE PRESENCE OF HER GOOD.

Love impresses on Rosa an inner impulse and moves her towards the Person loved. To be with her Good and to love him is for her superior to any other knowledge and earthly good.

The experience of the Presence of the Loved One is her supreme good. In her Good, with a knowledge that surpasses every human acquisition, she comes to know the prerogatives of her God, which often, unable to set them down in adequate words, she expresses in a phrase full of wonder:

“...I was caught up by my Good and felt great things! immense consolation...” (M. 1.1, p. 24).

The act of loving is certainly superior to the act of knowing. From the passage of the Memoirs that follows there radiates the experience of a page of the Gospel. It is an example of how the knowledge of the mysteries of faith comes about in mysticism (2):

“Holy Saturday; at the gladness that my Good showed, risen, I exulted. It was a something, stronger than myself; I could not restrain myself; I would have cried out to all to come with me to adore my Good, who already, beautiful and sweet, was walking about Risen; and to restrain the impulse a little, I began to sing loudly, but no, it grew in me. I would have wished to write beautiful things, but I was not able to hold them in my mind” (M. 1.1, p. 21).

Mystical experience is not confined to the contemplative gaze towards God, but is a process of interior transformation. The relationship to God or to the mystery of salvation urges the contemplative to an immediate participation in the divine life (3).

In this sense, in the experience reported below one notes how the presence of the Child Jesus creates in Rosa a movement of spiritual growth, of more faithful adherence to the life of God:

“I said to myself: oh, I will rest a little longer; but I did not think that I did not have the obedience to do so; so I remained, when a few minutes later the Child Jesus appeared to me. Oh! my Love, I am ready; ah, what have I done; how beautiful he was; he stayed a moment and came towards me with open arms and disappeared. Oh! my Love, yes, I am coming to receive you; and in haste I ran to the Church to receive him. Oh! what I felt! Say, my Good, you alone could tell it! Oh! you who are my Paradise! What can I do to make you known by the whole world. Oh! how many there are who do not know you, and those who have known you flee from you because they have never seen you; I would like to run everywhere and cry aloud for all to come and love you” (M. 1.1, p. 30).

The details of the context in which the mystical experiences take place become signs of the one language used by God to unveil his will to the person who is the object of his special love.

2. THE PROMISE OF JESUS COMES TRUE.

These ineffable moments nourish an ever higher perception of the Presence which Jesus has promised to the soul that loves him.

Rosa is one of these souls who, by loving him, merits the fulfillment of the promise of Jesus:

“Oh! my Love, what you make me feel in this Heart of yours. Oh! if man could come to understand what great things are felt in this Love, surely he would not hesitate one minute to put away those affections which soon wither.

Only your Love increases every day and, I will say it better, never has an end” (M. 1.1, p. 46).

She discovers that the secret of having her Good present is to associate herself with his redemptive mystery; for this reason she comes to the full acceptance of suffering:

“While I was in the fierce persecutions, behold my God who comes to comfort me. What was I to do but desire that others should come soon, since in this way my Good came to comfort me? Oh! your caresses!...”

“From all sides tribulations and pains rained down on me. But how could I feel them? not at all! In my love everything is absorbed by the sweetness of his Love. Yes, strike, for this donkey is tough, and my soul rejoices greatly. An indescribable calm. Last night, as I was about to take my rest, as usual on the cross, I felt myself caught up” (M. 1.1, p. 117; 157).

Because of her dedication she can hear the words of God as addressed to herself: “I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness” (Hos 2:22). Her faith in fact becomes more and more fidelity, adherence to the will of God. This adherence is all the more solid in that, within the soul, her Good bears witness to his own presence by means of a light which is a participation in the divine light. Rosa therefore walks the path of sanctification willed by Him, following the light.

Out of love she unites herself to her most holy God; by that very fact she is bound to sanctify herself; but since God is love, she understands that she must live in love (4).

In the description of her spiritual progress she attests that it is her Good who instructs and forms her:

“I believe it is the ugly monster; as soon as I had said this, the same Voice: try, and you will see that you will feel nothing. Oh Jesus, my Good, what am I to do?

The Voice again, with its usual gentleness: try, it is my desire; and then I said: no, this Voice is my Good, because I know it too well, and the ugly one who speaks to me dully is the dragon. And at once I put on, or rather I made myself these irons and then put them on. They were most atrocious points set on a skin, and I had nothing to feel, not even that night; they were most gentle pains. Oh! sweet Love, what did I receive as a gift? Oh! sweetness (caught up in Him I enjoyed the most beautiful and dear delights, illustrations); he taught me so many beautiful things” (M. 1.1, p. 138).

3. “WALK IN MY PRESENCE...”

Adherence to God, through love, opens the soul to receive a new light. On the new horizon it sees clearly the holiness of God and all that is out of harmony in itself and in others.

From this light there is born a new tension, which causes a suffering all the greater in that it makes the soul perceive the intensity of its natural attachments (5).

This is how Rosa describes this inner dynamism, the light that enlightens her and the witness of mercy of her Good:

“To suffer and to rejoice. Oh! how useful these lights are to me; in a flash I see everything. Oh! what I feel, how I feel myself all aflame, and I set about correcting that fault with such force, because it is an offense against my Good. Be silent, heartless ones; why do you offend my dear Crucified? What has he done to you that you should (offend him) so barbarously? I feel such pain at it, but Jesus is silent. Through the depths of his immense mercy he suffers and does not punish. Oh! my Love, so many times I beg him to take from me this pain that I suffer” (M. 1.1, p. 140).

The things which Jesus has heard from his Father (cf. Jn 15:15), and which he makes known to her in mystical union, must not be forgotten.

It is his words and his divine interventions that weave her personal history and that of the Work. These interventions and words, her Good insists several times, she must set down on paper. Since He is the light of her path, she obeys, even though she cannot foresee that this light will illumine the path of all those who will follow her in the ways of God.

From her testimony on this point we receive the confirmation:

“All for my Good, and so I remained many days and months without writing; but for this he gave me a just reproach, yet so gentle and sweet that I did not know what to answer, only: forgive me, my Good. – Tell me, why do you not write? – Oh! my Love, how can I? – At night, half an hour for a note, and then in time you will take it up again. – Oh! sweetness without equal; yes, my Good, I will not delay in doing it” (M. 1.1, p. 155).

Thanks to these written sources, born of obedience to Jesus, it is given to us to piece together the authentic history of Rosa with her Good and Lord. It is a profession of faith in Him, present in history, through which he continues to manifest himself to those who develop the capacity to perceive and contemplate his Presence.

In the life of Rosa Gattorno, from the beginnings of her widowhood, which may also be considered the experience and reason of her deep conversion to God, the Eucharist holds a privileged place. It is always central in her relationship with Jesus. Rosa soon discovers, beyond the sacramental signs, the real Presence of Christ, hidden from those who are unaccustomed to the contemplation of the Divine Mystery.

1. THE BLESSED SACRAMENT SHEDS BLOOD.

In the dialogue established with her, the Father, in order to assimilate her to the offering of the Firstborn Son, speaks to her through Jesus in the Eucharist with various signs which clearly refer to the symbolism of the history of salvation: blood, fire, light, flesh...

In the Gospel of Mark and of Matthew Jesus says: “This is my Blood of the Covenant...”, “poured out for many...”.

Jesus, in saying “this is my blood,” establishes a true relationship between the material element of wine and the mystery of his death. It remains beyond dispute that his words create a new situation in the common element of wine: they truly bring about a mysterious presence of Christ in the Church (1).

The Gospel texts offer us the criteria for interpreting the mystical datum of the vision of the “blood” in the Host seen by Rosa Gattorno:

“While the Blessed Sacrament was exposed for Benediction, I saw in the Most Holy Host the living Blood, which seemed to be pouring out...” (M. 1.1, p. 2).

“...they were about to give Holy Benediction, and the Blessed Sacrament was exposed. I saw the most precious Blood of my Good, and what did it produce in me? Oh! my Love! you alone could tell it, who were at work in me. I remained in ecstasy and did not know, could no longer say anything, and all that can be said is little and a nothing...” (M. 1.1, p. 12).

The mystical experience of the Blood in the Host is repeated with notable frequency; it fills her with blessedness, forms her to understand the nature of the mystery of Christ the Victim of the New Covenant, and makes her docile to letting herself be transformed by this aspect of the divine mystery:

“I saw in the Most Holy Host the Most Precious Blood...”.

“I saw the Blood in the Host; it was mingled with his Most Holy Flesh, so clearly was it shown to me.”

“...in the church of Our Lady of Graces... the Blessed Sacrament was exposed, and I saw the Most Holy Host dripping with blood and producing in me the same effects: contentment, peace, resignation to Suffering, strength to resist; and they were so marked that for a long time they remained impressed on me; a most lively, most ardent desire to undergo martyrdom for the faith and to be able to give vent to this thought and desire of mine...” (M. 1.1, p. 14; 16; 24). (2).

2. THE EUCHARIST, FOOD THAT GIVES LIFE.

What we believe by faith: that Jesus is truly and mysteriously present in the natural elements of bread and wine, is, for Rosa, an object of experience:

“One morning, in feeding on the Most Holy Flesh of my Love, I felt a taste so exquisite that I would not know how to explain it... it brought me an indescribable consolation” (M. 1.1, p. 18).

It is a vital necessity for Rosa to share daily in the Eucharistic Table, at which she is nourished by the Body and Blood of Christ, which invigorates and sustains her above all in the moments of spiritual struggle in which she remains alone with him (3):

“Only the strength which Jesus provided for me, of being able every day to feed on the Heavenly Bread...”.

“I went to make Holy Communion. What I felt, my Good,... I remained absorbed in him..., and when I came to myself I was so comforted, strong as a giant; I would have defied the whole world, the persecutions...” (M. 1.1, p. 9; 142).

From Him who willed to use as matter and symbol the elements which recall not only the primary food of life, but also the sharing of bread with the poor, she learns to love those who are alone and suffer: she burns with the desire to share with others the life she experiences in prayer:

“...in haste I ran to the church to receive him. Oh! what I felt! Say, my Good, you alone could tell it. Oh! you who are my Paradise! What can I do to make you known by the whole world? Oh, how many there are who do not know you, and those who know you flee from you because they have never seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry aloud for all to come and love you” (M. 1.1, p. 30).

In this desire of radical self-giving she anticipates what goes on maturing in the Eucharist over time: giving concrete form to the ends intrinsic to the Sacrament of the paschal mystery: “to make of all men one Family.”

In sharing in the Eucharist she goes on unifying her whole life, which is transformed into “light and salt of the earth,” helping to give its true face of love to a world disfigured by evil. It is this real participation, this effective sacrifice of her person, that allows Christ not to be confused with the sacrament, but rather to reveal himself through the Sacrament as the Eternal Presence that walks with humanity.

Rosa, in fact, in the sacrament unites herself to the presence, learning to live in God and for God alone.

3. EUCHARISTIC CELEBRATION.

The Eucharist does not recall death alone, but is open to life; it is not the commemoration of a dead man, but the exaltation of a living One who spreads for his own the table of the banquet in time, while awaiting that in which the Church will share in eternity.

The Eucharist, Jesus always with us!

In the words addressed to the apostles: “do this in memory of me,” it is held that Jesus meant that he should be remembered with the fullness of saving meaning which He willed to give to the institution of the Eucharist; that the Eucharistic institution should not remain an isolated event of history, but be made continually present with the effects and the demands of love contained in it (4).

With the extraordinary signs he made use of, Jesus impressed indelibly on Rosa’s soul the meaning and nature of this sacrament in the Church. Mystical experience introduced her into its essence, into the act performed by Him on the night of the Supper: “Now while they were eating, Jesus took bread and, having said the blessing, broke it and gave it to the disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my Body.’ Then he took the cup and, after giving thanks, gave it to them, saying:

“‘drink of it, all of you, for this is my Blood of the Covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’” (Mt 26:26-28). (5).

Trinitarian experience in the Eucharist.

The sign of bread and wine opens up and makes her pass from the vision of the mystery of the life of Christ himself to the Trinitarian life and to her involvement in the paschal reality of Christ:

“While I was hearing Holy Mass and offering to the Eternal Father the Sacrifice of the Altar, a most vivid light (6) appeared to me, together with a voice that said to me: this sacrifice of yourself in that Chalice together with His Beloved Son is very pleasing to God, but it would please him greatly if you offered yourself as a victim in all the Sacrifices that are celebrated on the altars of the whole Catholic world; and at once I did not delay in doing so; as soon as this was done I remained absorbed in God, and my intellect clearly saw all the sacrifices accomplished and to be accomplished in all the Catholic Churches. I rejoiced greatly, and so every morning I renew the offering: Behold, my God, your victim who unites herself to Jesus...” (M. 1.1, p. 123).

The Eucharist, Christ who makes himself present in it, involves her radically. The Trinity itself becomes present with interior words that reveal her mission, associated with that of the divine Victim, which opens her to universal horizons and directs her towards the ransom of sinners.

Her unconditional response to the Father’s demands makes her grow in love; the divine fire grows in her in adoration, in apostolic and universal zeal, in faith, in the understanding of the mystery which the Eucharist represents: victim with the Victim in the Trinitarian light, the Father’s good pleasure, offering, praise, thanksgiving, adoration which reach the universe and bring into the hearts of sinners the echo, the call, the demand for a new humanity for a new world according to God’s plan: “to make Christ the heart of the world.”

The Chalice.

The reference to the “Chalice” – “in that Chalice,” “I saw myself in a chalice” – set beside the words of Paul: “As often as you drink this cup...” (1 Cor 11:26) and the term “blood”: “I saw in the Host the most precious blood,” evokes the words of Jesus: “...this is my blood of the Covenant... poured out for the multitude.” These are words which refer back to the 4th song of the Servant of Yahweh: “He bore the sins of many and interceded for sinners” (Is 53:12). (7).

These references affirm that the Eucharist is the new Covenant in that it is the definitive and irrevocable self-dedication of God in Jesus Christ for us. It communicates to us, through the gift of the Spirit of Jesus, that self-giving of Jesus which makes us capable of living and dying as He lived and died.

In the Eucharist, therefore, the whole Old Testament history of God’s Covenants with his people is fulfilled in a sublime way: from the Eucharist is born the new people, the new children who form the Body of Christ, the Church (8).

The mission of the divine Victim is thus shown to be Rosa’s mission as well, because the symbols and words through which the Father instructs her are unmistakable:

“I saw myself in a most beautiful chalice, and as a Victim my soul was being offered to the Eternal Father; it was surrounded by a most vivid light; I came to myself and was furnished with strength to face all sacrifices” (M. 1.1, pp. 97-98).

As was noted earlier (M. 1.1, p. 123), her response was not slow in coming; she herself, almost repeating God’s gesture, places herself in the chalice as a victim:

“...I placed myself in that chalice, asking the Eternal Father to be pleased to look upon me, for I was covered, drenched with the Blood of my love Jesus. On the Altar of Sacrifice there are two victims, look upon us! and saying this I remained absorbed in God. He let me see that he had accepted that offering of the sacrifice with great pleasure...” (M. 1.1, p. 179).

It is evident that for Rosa the Eucharist is not only an act of worship; it is the living encounter with Christ the Victim, it is also the fullness of the encounter, exultation, the happiness of seeing the destinies of the world mature in Christ until all is recapitulated in Him:

“My intellect clearly saw all the sacrifices accomplished, to be accomplished... I rejoiced greatly” (M. 1.1, p. 123).

4. ADORING THE BLESSED SACRAMENT.

As a daughter of the Catholic Church, Rosa had been formed to profess the presence of Jesus under the sacramental species.

From the historical data we can deduce that, even before she was initiated by the Lord into the mystical language of the Eucharist, she used to stay and adore Jesus solemnly exposed in the churches of Genoa. The dimension of adoration, of the act of prayer which affirms the lordship of God and the utter dependence of man, asserts itself very early in her life.

The path of adoration.

The Lord forms her for exclusive love and fidelity to Jesus Crucified and Risen through the Eucharist. He who throughout the history of salvation has shown his jealousy for the act of adoration, requiring it exclusively for himself: “You shall not bow down before other gods,” traces out for Rosa the path of adoration.

The extraordinary signs associated with the Eucharistic presence, outside the context of the celebration, what can they indicate if not that she must adore, love, glorify and profess before the churches and the world the mystery of Christ, really present in the sacramental species of bread and wine?

Eucharistic Presence in the churches.

The way to please the Lord in this making herself present to Him by adoring him is shown to her mystically, as we go on to see:

“...suddenly a rapture so strong, and I found myself in spirit in a church where my Good had been exposed during the day. I saw the church all lit up, resplendent with light, an infinity of Angels adoring their God, my Beloved! I saw all the doors closed and found myself alone; I drew near the Tabernacle, and a throng of Angels was there; a light so vivid dazzled me. I saw my Beloved, of immense beauty; a fire burned in me...” (M. 1.1, p. 66).

Carried away by ecstasy, she finds herself several times adoring him in the chapels of the Institute or in one of the many churches (9), where he dwells among men and unites them to the Heavenly Church. In them, amid a splendor which transcends all natural brightness, she sees the adoring Angels and is also admitted to the vision of Paradise:

“...caught up in him I saw the church all a splendor, the good souls who had received him and many angels who nearby... were in the act of adoration...; greater was the light... that surrounded the ciborium, and in this light I saw the Sovereign Lady of Heaven...” (M. 1.1, pp. 152-153).

And on another date she writes:

“...yesterday, the day of the Body of the Lord, I was... in adoration, while... I was absorbed in God and... my Jesus who was saying to me: ‘look’ – I seemed to see all the souls of Paradise – ‘these are the ones who received me in life’...; they were of a most resplendent light...” (M. 3, p. 41).

Dwelling in him.

These mystical experiences transform her into Christ himself, who in the Eucharist handed himself over willingly to the consequences of the mission entrusted to him by the Father: death on a cross, in a context of abandonment by his own and of persecution and condemnation by the religious authorities. Jesus shows her his good pleasure by letting her experience the life that comes from the Sacrament of Love, giving her spiritual consolations during her long hours of adoration and enlightening her on the points on which she needs clarification:

“...so, my daughter, this is all my work, and it was the first thing I placed in your heart, the repugnance for all that is of worldly gratification” (M. 1.1, p. 130).

And he unites her to himself by drawing her mystically into the Tabernacle:

“...I remained absorbed, caught up in my Good, and he filled me wholly with strength; as soon as I felt myself caught up, it was then that I felt something, I know not what, torn out of me from the side of the heart; at once I found myself in him, and it seemed to me that I had flown inside the Tabernacle” (M. 1.2, p. 33).

Thus Rosa learns to make her dwelling in Him, in the Tabernacle, the tent of the new chosen people, the Church, in the dwelling place of the permanent presence of God among men:

“...I felt something torn out of me, from the side of the heart.”

The Father, who created Rosa to make her a sharer in the life of Christ and in his glory, acts in her with the power of his Spirit, purifying her, detaching her from all that is not divine and filling her with gifts: “to be holy and immaculate in charity” (cf. Eph 1:4).

The sense of the presence of the Spirit, as the gift of the Father poured into her at baptism, gradually changes into an ever deeper perception of the identity of the Spirit and of what he is bringing about in her.

The promises which Jesus made about the sending of the Spirit: “... the Father will give you another Consoler. You will know him, because he abides with you and will be in you” (Jn 14:16-17), are fulfilled in Rosa’s life and find in her a witness to the “indwelling” of the Consoler, who loves her and goes on shaping her according to the Father’s plan.

1. THE GRACE OF THE LORD.

The Holy Spirit, as he prepared Mary throughout the history of salvation and worked continually in her by grace, continues to act in every person. With the same grace he awakens faith and brings forth new life in Rosa, giving her an exclusive taste for God and a growing love for Jesus Crucified and for her neighbor (1). Rosa’s writings attest admirably to the working of grace in her person:

“...having been left free of every bond, I devoted myself with greater fervor to pious works and to visiting the hospitals and the sick poor in their homes, helping them in everything.

By the grace of the Lord I became aware that all earthly affections were fading away; nothing was any longer pleasing to me; my God alone was the pasture of all my delights. My sorrows... I poured into the heart of my Dear Crucified; for him alone, I kept repeating to myself, all my suffering is little, because I had committed many sins...” (M. 1.1, p. 1).

Moved by the grace of the Holy Spirit, she feels herself drawn by her dear Crucified, unified in her affections to the point of concentrating all her desires and tastes in God, purified, transformed and urged to grow in love. The life of the Spirit nourishes her, heals her, orders her activities, and sends her to serve those who suffer and to bear witness to the gift she has received.

The one who works in her, comes to the aid of her weakness, forgives her sins and intercedes for her needs is the Spirit (cf. Rom 8:26). (2).

2. THE SPIRIT, A CONSUMING FIRE.

The relationship of the Spirit with Rosa reveals the constant features of the Bible concerning his Presence in individual persons and in the life of the people and of the Christian communities.

The Holy Spirit never speaks of himself; he only lets himself be perceived and contemplated in relation to the divine persons of the Father and the Son. He makes known the secrets of God and of Christ his Word. He is known through his dynamism of love and of the sanctification of men. The world therefore cannot know him. He is known by whoever welcomes Christ into his life (3).

The description Rosa gives of her experience with the Spirit allows us to grasp this discreet presence in the movement that goes from the contemplation of the Face of Christ to the mysterious experience of the fire that devours and consumes her:

“...I saw the face of my Redeemer. Oh! how beautiful it was! What joy, my love! It was so luminous that I would not know how to explain its light and beauty. I felt myself all inflamed by that object which was consuming me. Ah! when will that day be on which, in so beautiful a moment, you, O my Good, will consume me?” (M. 1.1, p. 13).

The Spirit draws her to Jesus: he awakens in her as a devouring fire, but what in turn arouses this power of love is the sight of the Redeemer.

The Spirit, in fact, shows her in most splendid light the Face of her Redeemer, makes her fall in love with an irresistible attraction and with a strength that is no longer her own. Though present, he is overshadowed by Rosa’s act of love for her Redeemer. He is like a mother who brings her own child to life, giving herself that the child may live.

She therefore knows him in relation to Christ, by the light that illumines his face and by the fire which the very presence of Christ kindles in her (4).

The experience of the Presence of the Spirit as Love points to his Identity: the Third divine Person of the Trinity is Love, the essence of God himself: “God is Love...; by this we know that we abide in him and He in us: he has given us his Spirit,” “whoever abides in love abides in God and God abides in him” (1 Jn 4:8; 13; 16).

The Scriptures, with reference to the reality “Spirit-Love”: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom 5:5), offer a rich testimony.

The Spirit is Love who pours love into Rosa. She, like all Christians, is a temple of the God who is Love, and she herself becomes love in the gift of the Spirit, which includes all the other gifts (5):

“I find myself close to the Side of my Beloved, and what I felt... on feeling myself brought near to that Volcano of love...”.

“Your love consumes me; I feel burning in me a devouring flame that burns and consumes me.

A continual pang that I can no longer bear, yet I do not suffer, because the joy I feel is most delightful, without equal. But what comes over me is the fear that he may go away... Oh! what a wound I feel at the mere thought that I might, even inadvertently, displease him...” (M. 1.1, p. 41 ff.).

The Spirit who breaks in upon her as “fire” is, in Rosa’s mystical experience, a constant which sheds light, bringing out the centrality of Love in her relationship with the third Person of the Trinity.

The divine fire evokes various biblical images, expressions of the presence of the Spirit in individual persons and in the community: “John is that Elijah who is to come; the fire of the Spirit dwells in him and makes him run before the Lord who is coming”; “...on the day of Pentecost... there appeared to them tongues of fire which parted and rested on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit...” (Acts 2:1 ff.). (6).

Rosa too mystically experiences the Spirit as Love, a Fire dwelling in her, and attests to its ways in the pages of her spiritual memoirs:

“Oh! you are too sweet...; alas, a fire consumes me... it is... as if I had a furnace”;

“For several days the region of my heart has seemed about to open... the fire is burning...”;

“...the fire grew in me more and more, so much that I could not stand on my feet...”;

“...I thought I would die of the fire; union with my God was devouring me, so that I had to distract myself lest they should notice...”;

“The fire was devouring me; I felt a something on my left side (7), so that everything within me was moving, and this most sweet movement, when it comes to me, makes me die...” (M. 1.1, p. 120; M. 1.2, pp. 31; 46; M. 3, pp. 1; 23).

The gift of the Father, the Holy Spirit, did not exhaust his mission in Mary, the burning bush of the definitive theophany, full of grace, in whom by the power of his love he formed Jesus. He continued to be the Love, the power of the life, mission and resurrection of Jesus, and he continues in every person to transmit the Trinitarian life and to form in him a child of God.

Within the horizon of this mission of love lies his action in regard to Rosa, in whom he “indwells,” letting himself be experienced mystically as fire and shaping her with this fire in the image of Christ and of Mary (8).

In the ecstasies of love he introduces her into the intimacy of his divine essence:

“I spent the night clasped to my Good. Oh! joy! I was dying, so great was the love I felt. Not a single instant did I have outside of him. My Eternal all, who can describe what you do and communicate to the soul, and what it feels in you? Today in you, and you live for me. I feel that I have no life left but yours. A calm, an inner peace that I cannot describe. I speak, or rather I feel... my Spirit. I feel a something that is felt and not seen with bodily eyes, but the intellect sees and understands everything...” (M. 4.3, p. 16).

It is by this divine power that Rosa bears fruit in the Church and for humanity. Letting herself be shaped by the Spirit, she experiences the blessed consequences of his presence, the fruits of his grace: love and peace: the synthesis of joy, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22).

The Fire of God – Jesus “will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Lk 3:16), that Spirit of whom Jesus said: “I have come to bring fire upon the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled” (Lk 12:49) – is regarded by Christian tradition as the symbol, one of the most expressive, of the action of the Holy Spirit. For this reason Paul exhorts Christians, saying: “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thes 5:19). (9).

3. HOLY SPIRIT, DIVINE LIGHT.

The Holy Spirit perfects Rosa’s faith. The very One who has been at work since creation: “...the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Gen 1:2), and who spoke through the Prophets, dwells in Rosa’s inner being to teach her all things, as Jesus promised: “...the Holy Spirit whom the Father will send in my name, He will teach you all things and remind you of all that I have told you” (Jn 14:26). (10).

Approaching her writings leads us into her inner reality, flooded with the lights of the Spirit, who guides her with the Voice, with the gift of discernment (cf. M. 1.1, p. 63) and other signs at the moments of growth in holiness and at the decisive steps of the mission:

“...he always instructs me, admonishes me; oh, how severe he is in this. In the smallest things he warns me where I am failing, and it does not please him if I do not do such a thing at once...”;

“Oh, how many beautiful lessons he gave me. He explained certain doubts of mine, he showed me what I had to go through...” (M. 1.1, pp. 109; 144).

Christ, the Beloved, in the Spirit opens her mind (11) for the exercise of discernment in action and enlightens her on the essence and the degrees of love:

“I was instructed about a certain thing to be done. He taught me about his love, its degree and how it is communicated to the soul... I saw it all immense, great without equal. I saw how the soul, in order to receive this Love, must be well purified; thus it feels itself burning, being consumed, but the ardent longing grows, the ardent longing to be consumed and to burn still more. Oh, incomprehensible mystery: To suffer and to enjoy infinitely the delights of the Loved One! One always desires him alone, and for him everything is little. Yes, my Love” (M. 1.2, p. 45).

This experience of faith is possible in Rosa because she lets herself be guided by his Spirit. It is he who goes before her, giving her outward signs as well in support of the inner gifts (12):

“While... I was praying I felt a something that made me blessed... All at once, behold a most beautiful Light...”;

“I remained in him. In intimate union I enjoyed things that I am not able to express; when I came to myself there was before me a light which, wherever I went, was always near me, most beautiful,... it brought me gladness and peace” (M. 1.2, pp. 70; 80).

Rosa’s mystical experiences are often introduced by a light of greater or lesser intensity. This luminous sign points to the light that transcends every created light and is the vehicle of the Presence which it announces and reveals. Rosa makes explicit references to the light when she describes her mystical experiences with the other Persons of the Trinity, with Mary, with the Eucharist, and with other presences which are introduced to her awareness precisely by the light that precedes them (13).

The Holy Spirit of the promises (cf. Gal 3:14; Eph 1:13), who prepared the time of the Messiah by announcing him through the mouth of the prophets so that he might be awaited and welcomed at the moment of his manifestation (14), keeps Rosa’s hope awake by showing her the Work of God in its future fulfillment:

“In the distance I see many things, great ones, for our Institute. A Light let me see the great panorama of the order in the future; I will say that the divine ordering was so beautiful and so interwoven that I remained in ecstasy and rejoiced, while I also saw in it a stream of many sufferings. In that sight they did not frighten me at all...” (M. 3, p. 17).

4. THE SANCTIFYING SPIRIT.

The Spirit, the Paraclete (the One who is called to one’s side), sent by Jesus to all people to move them to love with all their heart, with all their soul and with all their strength, and who has come also to convince the “world concerning sin” (Jn 16:8), is Rosa’s interior teacher (15).

She specifies, in her Memoirs, that the Spirit guides, enlightens and purifies her on the path of sanctification:

“Oh, my Love! I remained caught up in him: what I saw, what I felt...! He showed me certain imperfections; although I know that I am a heap of infamies, yet in that union my Good washes my poor soul, which is left purified in the fire of his divine Love. Oh! sweetness!...” (M. 1.2, p. 118).

On another page, describing union with her God, she adds:

“...I was left so convinced of my nothingness... that it seemed to me I no longer had the courage to stay in the presence of my God...; the more intimate the union became, the more I discovered my nothingness...”;

“...I was distressed because I had no one to whom I could say a word. A Voice said to me: ‘why do you say this? do you not remember what I told you a short time before such a defeat reached you from Rome? I am your Teacher, be at peace. The peace of conscience which I enjoy in the midst of so many tribulations... is such that I see there is a most powerful Spirit who rules me...’” (M. 3, p. 21; M. 4.1, p. 4).

Rosa is conformed to Christ by this Presence dwelling in her, which animates her, upholds her, goes before her and accompanies her in the fulfillment of her vocation to holiness (16).

5. THE SPIRIT AND THE MISSION.

The Holy Spirit, whom the Father reveals through his mission in time: in creation, in the word of the Prophets, in the Incarnation of the Word in the womb of Mary, in the life of the Son and in his work, in the preaching and work of the Apostles after the glorification of Jesus, fully manifests the fullness of the Trinitarian mystery and continues his work in the mission of the Church.

His mission unfolds from then on in the children adopted by the Father in Christ Jesus (17).

The life and mission of Rosa, as a daughter in the Son, are therefore a mystical place of the Presence and mission of the Spirit.

Her “time” – the stretch of history entrusted to her by the Father – was a time of the Spirit and of witness, but also a time marked by various needs and by trials which did not spare her, a time of vigilance and trusting expectation (18).

On every page of her Memoirs the presence of the Spirit in her life and mission is attested:

“...but He who governs and works in this very work of his knows well how to take away and to give everything at his good pleasure... the mental illustrations became much clearer and more vivid to me, so much so that, to my astonishment, I feel such sublime words coming from my mouth, and I find everything easy: to preach, to expound and to resolve whatever is asked of me...” (M. 3, p. 1).

And on another page she continues the description of this mystical Presence in her life and mission, which appears as a wonderful interweaving of the work of the Spirit and of her own participation:

“I feel, and with greater clarity I see myself guided by my dear Spirit...”;

“I was always acting, but I did not know how or why I acted... I did everything, not I, but the one who lives in me: I felt that I was answering and did not know what. I saw everything going in order and did not know who was ordering it. I, in truth, was not capable, because... a tight crown seemed to encircle my head...” (M. 3, pp. 11; 13).

The Holy Spirit not only works in her, for her and with her, but also consoles her on her pilgrimage towards the Kingdom with signs and symbols which in the Old and New Testaments overshadow and reveal his Presence (19).

“One day I was working; I saw coming from on high a very beautiful Dove, and it seemed to be coming straight to strike me on the forehead, but as soon as it brushed me it disappeared. After a few moments a beautiful Light...” (M. 1.1, p. 69 f.).

In Rosa’s mystical experiences with the Holy Spirit, the perception of love as living fire, of the gift of understanding, of discernment, of fortitude (cf. M. 1.1, p. 144; M. 1.2, p. 2; M. 3, p. 11) and of all the other gifts brought out in her writings is joined by the vision of signs and symbols (light, voice, dove, cloud) (20), which play a specific role in identifying her particular vocation and mission in God’s plan.

THE CLOUD.

As the people of the Bible were guided by God: He himself, in fact, through the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire shared in the wanderings of his people, so Rosa, for some years of her life, is guided by the cloud of the Lord.

1. THE CLOUD MANIFESTS THE LORD.

She experiences the presence of her Beloved in the Cloud, from which there comes a voice that consoles her, reassures her and enlightens her in her doubts:

“Now I consult my cloud. Always, every time I am in need, it counsels me, answers me what I must do, how I must conduct myself, and I feel myself comforted in adversities. Oh! last night I saw what beauty there was within It” (M. 1.1, p. 85).

In the light of Revelation the mystical symbol becomes clear through which the Lord speaks to Rosa in order to accompany her during the fundamentally important stage of the foundation. Sacred Scripture, which is the source of reference for the Church, serves as our guide in the study of Rosa’s experience with the Cloud.

Exodus offers an ample description of the presence of God through the cloud (1): “The Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they might travel by day and by night. Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night withdrew from the sight of the people” (Ex 13:21-22).

Although she finds herself in a historical situation different from the conditions of the pilgrim people of the Exodus, Rosa lives a religious experience of similar spiritual content, meant to direct her path in God and that of all who form the Family which God has entrusted to her:

“...in the midst of so great a tumult of an abyss of affairs, yet I am never deprived of union with my God; indeed for some time now, since he furnished me with that dear treasure which I always see at my side, and it is a cloud, something beautiful; one sees that it contains a being, because, as I said above, I have already seen him...” (M. 1.1, pp. 86-87).

In the verse of the book of Exodus already cited, one notes how during the long marches in the desert the chosen people was preceded by the Lord with the pillar of cloud.

The testimony of the people, who saw the glory of the Lord like a devouring fire in the cloud (cf. Ex 16:10), shows how the cloud is subordinate to the manifestation of the Lord. The cloud makes perceptible the nearness of God the Liberator, the Savior, the one Lord of his people.

2. THE CLOUD POINTS TO THE TRANSCENDENCE OF GOD.

The cloud, however, also has, by its opacity, the characteristic of bringing out the divine transcendence, inaccessible to man unless God himself draws near to him.

In other words, the cloud, now dark, now luminous, reveals the living and saving God while veiling the transcendence of his glory (2).

Of the luminosity of the cloud Rosa speaks to us thus:

“Each time it becomes denser and rosier, and a voice comes forth which puts me in paradise, and I remain absorbed. It tells me how I must conduct myself; when I do not know what to do or answer, I consult it and it answers me; I stop and look at it, I ask it: prompt me, for I do not know what to say, my being, my dear Love! Because I am convinced that it is He who is within, and I hear the Voice” (M. 1.1, pp. 87-107).

Experience, language, style and discernment evoke the experience of the Exodus, when the people went into the tent to consult the Lord: “When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and stand at the entrance of the tent. Then the Lord would speak with Moses... face to face, as one man speaks with another” (Ex 33:9-11).

3. THE CLOUD PRESENT AT THE TRANSFIGURATION OF JESUS.

The manifestations of God through the Cloud in Exodus are referred to throughout the whole history of Salvation. Moreover, other experiences come to confirm the theological value of the Cloud, the mysterious place of God’s presence: “The glory of the Lord, in the form of a Cloud, filled the Temple built by Solomon” (1 Kgs 8:10 f.). In Isaiah: “...the doorposts shook at the voice of the One who cried out, while the temple was filled with smoke” (Is 6:4).

On the day of the transfiguration of Jesus, the apostles, after contemplating “Moses and Elijah speaking with Jesus of his departure, which he was to accomplish in Jerusalem” (Lk 9:30), enter the cloud, and “from the bright cloud there came a voice that said: this is my beloved Son, listen to him” (Mt 17:5; Mk 9:7; Lk 9:34).

The presence of Moses and Elijah represents the Old Testament, which bears witness to the passion of the Servant. The figure of the Servant reappears in the voice and in the theophany associated with the cloud (cf. Ex 24:15-16; 40:34-38). Luke means that in Jesus and in his action God is present and intervenes, that God is pleased with Jesus’ acceptance of his suffering messiahship. And since the Cloud indicates the presence of the Spirit, the whole Trinity was present at the Transfiguration. The Father in the voice, the Son in the man, the Spirit in the bright cloud (3).

Guided by the light that radiates from this message, and in particular by the other verse of the same passage:

“And while he was praying, his face changed in appearance and his clothing became white and dazzling,” we read the passage that follows:

“That cloud which I used to see frequently, I now see more rarely. The other evening it appeared to me much more luminous than usual; while it stood before me and dazzled me, behold it expands and I see my Beloved in it: he was within It, he was of infinite beauty, of a splendor that I do not know what to compare it to. What he says to me, what he brings me! It sweetened all my pains, it made me forget everything. The tribulations, although they were not few, nothing of them is remembered. My love alone had absorbed everything; he left me something that I cannot explain, but I feel it in me, which makes me die of love! From all sides tribulations and pains were raining down, but how could I feel them! Not at all! In my love everything is absorbed by the sweetness of his love” (M. 1.1, p. 157).

4. THE CLOUD, SYMBOL OF GLORY.

Following further the traces of the Cloud-light symbolism, one sees how this presence is linked to other decisive events in the life of Jesus. It is the same cloud that takes him from the sight of the disciples on the day of the Ascension: “and a cloud took him from their sight” (Acts 1:9). “Jesus’ final apparition ends with the irreversible entry of his humanity into divine glory, symbolized by the cloud and by heaven, where He is seated from that time forward at God’s right hand.” (4).

The glorious return of Christ prophesied by the author of the Book of Revelation refers to the presence of the clouds, which however will not veil the face of the Lord, because He will be seated upon them: “I looked again, and behold a white cloud, and on the cloud sat one like a Son of man” (Rev 14:14). (5).

Another vehicle of the Father’s dialogue for showing Rosa his will is a Voice: it speaks to her, making known to her the contents of the mission she must carry out in the Church and the ways of fulfilling it, the constitutive elements of her identity and holiness in Christ.

1. THE VOICE LIGHTS UP HER PATH.

It is a distinct Voice which transcends the voice of her conscience, even though it respects and forms it. A Voice that awakens the values with which the Lord already endowed her in creating her. A Voice that directs her path, reassures her in doubt and demands offering of her. A Voice loved, loving, unmistakable, clearly distinguished by Rosa among the other voices which draw her away from the will of God. A Voice awaited, transforming, at once respectful and authoritative, a Voice that manifests the prerogatives of God and the aspects of the Mystery of Christ, a Voice that confirms the existence and presence of her Well-Beloved, of the Beloved, of the Spirit, of the Father:

“A Voice which was certainly his, my Good’s, said to me: from you I want this work. Take to the Archbishop the writing you have” (M. 2, p. 11). (1)

2. THE VOICE DIRECTS HER.

It is a Voice that forms Rosa to identify herself with Jesus Crucified:

“A loud Voice said to me: why do you speak so and complain so much? Do you see, to come to have what you say? There appeared to me a body all wounds. These are all penances, and it has suffered every kind of torment. And this one alone will have what you ask of me... Oh, my love, I will submit...” (M. 1.1, p. 104).

It forms her to trust in Providence and to love the will of God, which is manifested also through events:

“A Voice said to me: ‘Rosa, you know that all you want I will give you, and everything will be granted to you. If you knew what you possess and what I have given you; but no, it is not yet the hour. What you feel is only a very small part of what you could feel’” (M. 1.1, p. 118).

It obliges her to an ever more radical commitment in the Church and in the world:

“Often a Voice would say to me: ‘you must work..., it is time to go to work’; and as soon as I hear this I go at once, flying, although it costs me not a little. Oh, yes, I can say that my Beloved Jesus lives for me!” (M. 1.1, p. 116).

Thus she is sent to proclaim to her brothers and sisters the Presence that has made her grow, freeing her from human conditioning and enriching her with gifts.

The Voice corrects her when she falls into excesses of guilt, because she attributes the absence of her Good to her own failings:

“An inner Voice told me that my despair did not please it, but I am always with Him” (M. 2, p. 131).

It makes her attentive to the masterpiece of the Spirit:

“It was midnight and I went to the church, tired, exhausted...; kneeling, I began to meditate, resting my head on the wound of his shoulder, and inwardly I was afflicted because of certain cruel persecutions. A Voice said to me: ‘These will soon end like the others, and you will have what you desire’...” (M. 1.1, p. 143).

The Voice helps her to advance spiritually to the measure of Christ, who “gave himself for us, offering himself to God as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance” (Eph 5:2):

“A Voice that said to me: ‘This sacrifice of yours is very pleasing to God, but it would please him greatly if you offered yourself as a victim in all the sacrifices that are celebrated on the altars of the Catholic world’...”;

“...I intend to shun nothing, neither pains, nor sorrows, nor sacrifices; whatever the martyrdom may be, let every sword that pierces me as it pleases you be always turned towards me, towards me who am your victim. A Voice that said to me: ‘Yes, you are’...” (M. 1.1, pp. 123; 171).

3. THE VOICE ASKS FOR ADHERENCE TO GOD’S PLAN.

It forms her to walk in step with God, who shows in his interventions that his will is inexhaustible, that the final end towards which he is leading her is known to Him alone, that she cannot be content with having the certainty of norms approved by human authority. Rather, she must open herself each day to the newness of the Spirit.

She understands early, through the Voice, that the will of God sends her where she could not have imagined. She listens like Abraham: “Go from your country, from your homeland and from your father’s house, to the land that I will show you” (Gen 12:1), and follows the path indicated by God.

At the moment of the decision to found the Institute in Piacenza, assailed by the doubt that what she was living might be an illusion and might not correspond to the will of God, in prayer she hears:

“A clear Voice: ‘All that happened is my will; be at peace, be at peace, everything will be made smooth’” (M. 2, p. 47).

Rosa silently loves and adores her God, who goes on revealing himself through the Voice. She finds herself living, perhaps without being aware of it, the experience of Moses, who hangs on the Voice (Ex 3:4) of “the One who is” in order to face the risks of the mission, the responsibility (Ex 5:22-23) of guiding and governing a people with a law (Ex 19:20) towards holiness, the concern to give water and food to those who thirst and hunger (Ex 16:17), the unforeseen events of the long and wearisome journey (Ex 33:7-17; 34 ff.). As with Isaiah: “A Voice says: ‘Cry out’... lift up your voice, do not fear” (Is 40:6-9), and as the Voice requires other prophets to announce the future, to affirm the will of God and to denounce errors, so to her too it makes known in advance events or calamities, so that she may take part in them with her prayer. Through the Voice the Lord communicates to her his love for man:

“A Voice answered me: ‘Yes, I love man immensely’...”.

“...You, if one may say so, are mad with love for man, and he? A Voice that says to me: ‘Yes, I love him greatly’” (M. 1.1, p. 152; M. 1.2, p. 1).

4. THE VOICE FORMS HER FOR DISCERNMENT.

The tone, the style, the sweetness and firmness of the Voice form Rosa to distinguish exactly whether it comes from her God or whether instead it comes from the whisperer. She becomes ever wiser “in every kind of discernment” (Phil 1:9).

“A voice that was saying to me loudly: now you are dead..., brought me an ugly feeling, as of fright... Ah! I understand well, this is none other than the enemy...” (M. 1.1, p. 139).

By responding docilely to the Voice she becomes God’s delight. Mystical experience leads her to identify, “with all wisdom and spiritual understanding” (Col 1:9), the Voice with the will of God which is manifested to her, which is the strength of her freedom and the purpose of her life.

Her faithful response to the Voice makes her glad, grateful, firm in faith, persevering in hope, strong in the struggles of life and against the devil. The word spoken by the Voice takes flesh in her and in the events she directs: “It is I who live for you”; it becomes history. She seeks this Voice and waits for it to speak, and the Voice lets itself be found and heard. She knows no other knowledge than that of her Voice. She is “the humble slave of her beloved master.”

The Father, in his free initiative, raises Rosa to a share in his divine life through the direct action of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and breaks into her history with extraordinary interventions which enlighten her about her mission in the Church and for the world.

With this privileged Trinitarian action of his he associates the special mediation of Mary and of certain members who, in the communion of the Holy Spirit, are to help her on the path of personal sanctification and in the development of the plan entrusted to her for proclaiming and spreading the Kingdom of Christ (1).

1. IN THE CHURCH TO PROCLAIM THE KINGDOM OF GOD.

Through the contemplation of the divine mysteries and listening to the Voice, which in her inner being formulates a precise desire of the Father:

“INCREASE OF THE FAITH.”

Rosa experiences the dynamism which the Spirit impresses on the Church and on each of her members so that the purpose for which the world was created may be fulfilled. The Father, in fact, created it for the sake of the Church and of communion with his divine life, a communion which is brought about through the proclamation and the welcoming of salvation (2).

As Jesus began his Church by preaching the Good News, the coming of the Kingdom of God promised for centuries in the Scriptures, so Rosa, keeping alive the words suggested to her in secret: “Increase of the Faith,” gathers her strength to hand herself over to the cause of her Good.

A living member of the Church, a “branch united to the vine,” she sacrifices herself with love and for love to the Father’s plan (3).

Rosa finds in the Church the support for making the gift of herself to her God.

Jesus endowed his Church with a structure: the authority of Peter with the other Apostles, which will remain until the full accomplishment of the Kingdom.

The Apostles, in fact, share in the mission of Jesus, in his power, but also in his lot. Through the authority of the successors of Peter and of the Apostles, the Word of the Father, even if at times not easy to understand and accept, is confirmed to Rosa.

The decisive response to her call, to be a living stone of the holy building of Christ, is prompted by the command of the Lord, who sends her to submit to the directives of Ecclesiastical authority:

“Take to the Archbishop the writing you have” (M. 2, p. 11).

“...as soon as he had read them (the Rules), he (Monsignor Charvaz) wrote to me to come to him... and, knowing my character, he limited himself to telling me to try to carry out the orders of the Lord, and that the work will certainly be very beautiful...” (M. 2, p. 13).

For greater inner clarity she also goes to Pope Pius IX and, after confiding to him her family concerns, receives the further painful confirmation that she must obey:

“Pius IX blessed me and, having raised me up with his hand, which held mine tightly, told me that he had read those rules, and that they were truly beautiful, and that I must not put off carrying them out...” (M. 2, p. 23 f.).

And she continues with other words which the Pope adds on noting her perplexity laden with sorrow:

“...if you do not do what God wants of you, you will have remorse for it all the days of your life... ‘Your Holiness,’ I answered him..., ‘I want to do the will of God...’.

He went on... as if inspired: ‘This Institute will spread rapidly, like the flight of the dove, to all parts of the world... God will take care of your children; you, think of God in his work.’ What a prophecy!” (M. 2, p. 25 f.).

Christ, the one mediator, through his Church, at once visible and spiritual, with the authority of Pius IX, confirms Rosa and sustains her faith and fortitude in accepting and interpreting the inspiration received, and in fulfilling the will of the Father (4).

2. IN THE CHURCH AND AS CHURCH: BRIDE, SISTER AND FRIEND.

The Church is in history, but at the same time she transcends it. Only at the level of faith can she be perceived and penetrated in her mystical reality, the bearer of divine life (5).

Christ fulfills and reveals his Mystery as the goal of God’s design: “to recapitulate all things in Christ,” that is, to live one life with him, to share in his divine life and to bring about spousal union with him.

He, in fact, by his blood established a spousal bond with the Church, who, united to him as her bridegroom, becomes in her turn a mystery, a sacrament of him before all peoples (6).

To be transformed into Christ is the goal towards which all the members of the Church are striving. All the sacramental means are ordered to the holiness of the members. And holiness is measured according to the great mystery in which the bride responds with the gift of love to the gift of the Bridegroom.

Rosa lets herself be wholly drawn into this love. She clearly lives the Marian dimension in her life, knowing that Mary is the privileged member of the Church who fully realized communion in Christ: she is the perfect bride, sister and friend of the other members of the body of Christ as well (7). To her, therefore, she entrusts herself, to her maternal presence and guidance, so as to belong wholly to God and wholly to her brothers and sisters.

3. CHRIST ENTRUSTS HER MISSION TO HER IN THE CHURCH.

Union with Christ is, for every baptized person, spousal belonging and sending. It becomes a sacrament of the unity of the human race with its Creator and Father.

The unity already begun with the Paschal mystery of Christ must be prolonged through the Church and through every member of the Church. The disciple of Christ must reach out into the world so that there may be gathered around him “people of every nation, race, people and tongue” (8): “And Jesus, drawing near, said to them: ‘All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the world...’” (Mt 28:18-20).

As the Church, in the hands of Christ, is the instrument of redemption for all, the universal sacrament of salvation, so Rosa, being a living member of the Church – in this sense the whole life and mission of the Church is in her, and her personal life and mission is in the life of the Church – reveals by proclaiming it, and at the same time brings about, the mystery of God’s love for man (9).

Within the horizon of the words of Jesus, addressed to all disciples of every age, there stand out those spoken for her alone while she is absorbed in the presence of the Crucified:

“They shall devote themselves to the increase of our holy faith; to the care of the sick...; they shall receive... among them girls in danger and shall teach Christian doctrine...” (10).

4. THE FATHER APPOINTS HER GUIDE, OF A PRIVILEGED PORTION OF THE CHURCH.

So that Rosa may carry out her mission, the Holy Spirit provides her with various charismatic gifts. Furnished with the divine gifts, and in fidelity to the inspirations of the Spirit, she receives the strength to proclaim and intensify the Kingdom of God among various peoples (11).

It is a mission to be carried out with a portion of the Church (daughters and sons) which she receives as a gift from her Savior. The whole Church, in fact, was born of the total gift of Christ, anticipated in the Eucharist and accomplished on the cross (12).

Jesus grants her the perception of how he is the Lord of the Church and above all of how he infinitely loves and nourishes each of her parts and members:

“...when Holy Communion was made, my Savior appeared to me and showed me his heart: it was so great that I cannot describe it, and with his arm, resting on it, he was holding up a great thing that I cannot describe. He said to me: this is my Work, this Institute is my Work, and he clasped it. He told me so many things, and also that my suffering was pleasing to him...” (M. 12.2, p. 53 f.).

Suffering and love mark the development of the work entrusted to her, just as they characterized the Work of Christ.

The Church therefore will not have her fulfillment except in the glory of heaven, at the moment of Christ’s glorious return; until that day she continues her pilgrimage amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God. Here below she feels herself in exile, far from the Lord. The fulfillment of the Church in glory will come about through many trials. Then all the just will be united in the universal Church (13).

5. COMMUNION IN CHARITY.

The experiences of the pre-paschal Christ must mark Rosa’s life so that she may build up the portion of the people entrusted to her and, in it and with it, the Church.

Jesus is at root the holy Remnant, the Servant, the Son, the temple, the firstborn of the new people; “God with us,” the kingdom to come already placed in our midst.

At a first stage, therefore, the Church lives conversion to him, sets out to follow him, accepts the constitutive elements of his Covenant, becomes Jesus himself who takes upon himself the sins and the responsibilities of humanity (14).

Rosa is wholly drawn by God into the dynamism of this being immersed in the historical vicissitudes of the Church and in her mystical sorrow:

“The thought of what the Church was suffering was most painful to me, and at moments I fainted, so strong was the pain. The Head of the Church imprisoned, Pius IX, my father! Oh, what torment!... I always feel myself fainting, I am in agony; what will it be, my Good, do you leave me so, do you say nothing to me?...”.

“...I saw the Holy Mother veiled (I saw the picture covered with a veil). Oh, what pain I felt for two days!... at the end of the two days I saw her as usual, without a veil. I begged her so much to tell me something. A sorrowful voice said to me: Rome, the great tribulations” (M. 1.2, pp. 29; 31).

The initiative of sharing intensely in the mystery of the Church is often God’s, and so it is not given to her at once to see and understand what she is living:

“I am in the utmost desolation: horrible temptations against the Church. And who? My God, I am a monster of infamy! whereas for the Pope and the Cardinal Princes, the Bishops, what would I not do?

My life is a nothing to offer for the prosperity of the Church. Alas! how painful this state is to me!” (M. 5.2, p. 46).

She thus experiences in herself the echo of the sins of others, and the torment of fearing that it is she herself who wills and harbors certain feelings against the Church. And she is also called to share mystically in the passion of the mystical Body of Christ.

Jesus himself enlightens her, as she herself writes, on the meaning and value of her experiences in the Church:

“What I have suffered, my God! First there came upon me something that I cannot describe, and I said: ‘O my Love! what is this that I feel?’ ‘They are the pains which the Church is suffering’” (M. 5.3, p. 74 f.).

She can say with Paul: “none of us lives for himself and none of us dies for himself” (Rom 14:7). “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. Now you are the body of Christ and his members, each one for his part” (1 Cor 12:26-27). “Charity does not seek its own interest” (1 Cor 13:5).

6. COMMUNION WITH THE SAINTS.

Rosa receives from the Father the gift of living a special communion with certain Angels and Saints in particular.

She frequently enjoys the beneficial fruits of the intercession and protection of Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate, of Saint Francis of Assisi, of Saint Joseph, spouse of Mary Most Holy, of the Venerable Father Bernardo Maria Clausi, and of others who appear on her mystical horizon as messengers of the Lord.

Union with the Angels and Saints unites Rosa more intimately to Christ, from whom, as from its fountain and head, issue all the joy and all the life of the People of God itself (15).

Another dimension of her life and mission in relation to the Church is her mystical experience with those brothers and sisters who, having passed from this life, find themselves in a state of purification.

Her experiences of these presences in moments of prayer and solitude are frequent. It is the Father himself who allows these brothers and sisters to present themselves in order to ask her for prayers and penances on their behalf (16).

Rosa experiences the truth of what the Church has recognized from the earliest times of the Christian religion, that “it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from their sins” (2 Mc 12:44-46).

The efficacy of her prayers attests that God, by the work of the Holy Spirit, restores grace to sinners by virtue of the Redemption, and gives to the dead a share in the divine life that will have no end.

For this reason she offers suffrages for the dead with greater fervor and shares in their suffering in order to relieve it.

The Father shows her that her prayer not only helps them, but also makes their intercession on her behalf effective (17).

Mary, the beloved daughter of the Father, associated with the saving mystery of Christ, enters Rosa’s life as Mother, Teacher, Guide and Sister.

The mystery of Mary is present in her person as a gift of the Father, which helps her to understand better her vocation and mission in the economy of redemption.

In Mary, whom Rosa delights in calling: “my life, after my God,” “sweetest Mamma, Mother of my Love,” the Father goes on showing her, through visions and interior locutions, which aspect of the mystery of Christ she must in a particular way embody, proclaim and serve in the Church.

1. MARY ASSOCIATED WITH THE SUFFERING OF JESUS, AND THE EUCHARIST.

Rosa lives with fervor and dedication the feasts and memorials which the Church celebrates in honor of Mary. But it is the Father who introduces her in a special way into a fuller understanding of her privileges and of her role in the mystery of Christ.

With the clarity that comes to her from the Spirit, she describes the mystical experience in which the presence of Mary is closely connected with the Eucharist, with the Blood of the Redeemer, with the graces she is able to grant her:

“I received great graces from Mary Most Holy. While the Blessed Sacrament was exposed for benediction, I saw in the Most Holy Host the living Blood, which seemed to be pouring out...”.

“...in the novena of the Immaculate... I laid everything at the feet of Mary, that She might make a gift of it to my Good, Jesus, and beg him to accept me as his bride...; what I felt! as if I had entered into another state of living...” (M. 1.1, p. 2).

In Mary, associated with the life of her Son, Rosa comes to know more deeply the mystery of the poverty of Christ, in which she becomes so involved that it becomes a necessity for her to share in the suffering of his sorrowful life.

In the description of the mystical states in which one grasps the passage from union with Mary to the contemplation of the suffering Jesus, one perceives that configuration to Him comes about through a painful sharing:

“One day... I was reciting the office of the most blessed Virgin. Oh, what did I see! Close to me, my Jesus bound, with his hands behind him.”

“...strongly united and caught up in Mary..., so many times I saw the room and heard Mary’s weeping...; what I felt on seeing Jesus weep” (M. 1.1, pp. 11; 36).

The infused gift enlightens her about the relationship of the Mother with the Son; a relationship which leaves its mark on her life and mission, transforming her into the image of the One who stands in a perfect way beside the Son.
